description: "Four words everyone thinks they know — to love God, to know Him, faith, belief. The dictionary makes them inward and invisible: information, feeling, mental assent. Scripture binds all four to one covenant response without flattening them into synonyms: love is self-giving covenant allegiance embodied in commandment-keeping; faith is trust held steady through obedience in hope of the promise; belief receives God's word as governing truth and submits to it; knowing is the covenant relationship proved by the keeping."
og_title: "Love, Knowing, Faith, and Belief — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "This is the love of God, that we keep his commandments: and his commandments are not grievous."
    ref: "1 John 5:3"
---
Four words carry most of what people mean by being right with God: to _love_ Him, to _know_ Him, to have _faith_, to _believe_.
The dictionary has quietly emptied all four.
Knowledge becomes information; love becomes a feeling; faith and belief become assent — things held in the head and the heart, invisible, asking nothing of the hands.
By those definitions a man may know, love, believe, and have faith, and keep not one commandment.

Scripture will not allow it.
All four meet in one covenant response — the commandments kept — but they are not interchangeable synonyms.
Each holds a distinct office:

.One covenant response, four offices — and the word for holding them
[.prevalence-table%unbreakable, frame=topbot, grid=none, cols="2,7"]
|===
| *Love* | self-giving covenant allegiance embodied in the keeping
| *Knowing* | the covenant relationship proved by the keeping
| *Faith* | trust held steady through obedience in hope of the promise
| *Belief* | receiving God's word as governing sym:sym-truth[truth] and submitting to it
| *Faithful* | allegiance kept *consistent* — over time, under weight
|===

This chapter proves each office in turn.

[discrete]
=== Love

Begin where the confusion is thickest.
Love, we are told, is chiefly what you feel.
Scripture insists that love take a body:

[quote.scripture, 1 John 5:3]
____
For this is the *love of God, that we keep his commandments*: and his commandments are not grievous.
____

Jesus says it plainly: __“If ye love me, keep my commandments”__ (John 14:15).
And John's second epistle runs the whole chain in three verses, and swears none of it is new:

[quote.scripture, "2 John 4-6"]
____
I rejoiced greatly that I found of thy children *walking in* sym:sym-truth[truth], as we have received a *commandment* from the Father… not as though I wrote a *new commandment* unto thee, but that which we had *from the beginning*, that we love one another. And *this is love, that we walk after his commandments*…
____

Walking in sym:sym-truth[truth] and walking after His commandments are one walk — for __“thy law is the truth”__ (Psalm 119:142) — and the commandment that defines love is expressly *not new*: it is __“from the beginning”__ — _archē_, the very word that opens Genesis in the Greek Bible, and John's gospel after it.
The commandment to love is as old as creation.
Nor was it new when Moses wrote it: loving Him is __“to keep the commandments of the LORD”__ (Deuteronomy 6:5; 10:12-13).

These verses do not reduce love to a naked outward motion.
Paul says a man may give all his goods and even his body, yet lack love (1 Corinthians 13:3); John says __“God is love,”__ manifested when He sent His Son (1 John 4:8-10).
God is not obeying a superior.
The common center is self-giving covenant allegiance; for the creature under God's authority, that allegiance has a commanded body — obedience.
Warmth may accompany love, but it cannot substitute for it.
A deed severed from allegiance can be empty sacrifice; an allegiance that persistently refuses His commands is a false profession.

[discrete]
=== The Love Chapter, Read with the Symbols

Jesus was asked which commandment is greatest, and His answer hangs the whole canon on love:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 22:37-40, NKJV]
____
“You shall *love* the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.” This is the first and great *commandment*.
And the second is like it: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
On these two commandments *hang all the Law and the Prophets*.
____

Two loves, two tables of the same stone: the first four commandments are how one loves God; the last six are how one loves a neighbor.
The Law does not compete with love; it *hangs from it* — and love without the commandments is a hook with nothing on it.

Paul's hymn to love is quoted at weddings as if it were a mood; read it with the symbols and it is a legal argument.

[quote.scripture, 1 Corinthians 13:1-3, NKJV]
____
Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not *love*, I have become *sounding brass* or a *clanging cymbal*.
And though I have the gift of prophecy, and sym:sym-understanding[understand] all mysteries and all sym:sym-knowing[knowledge], and though I have all sym:sym-faith[faith], so that I could remove sym:sym-mountain[mountains], but have not love, I am *nothing*.
And though I bestow all my goods to feed the sym:sym-poor[poor], and though I give my body to be burned, but have not love, it profits me *nothing*.
____

Tongues, prophecy, mysteries, knowledge, sym:sym-mountain[mountain]-moving faith — every prized gift in the assembly, weighed and found to be *noise* without love.
This chapter has already located love's commanded body: __“this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments”__ (1 John 5:3).
Read it so, and the audit is exact: spectacular gifts and even self-chosen sacrifice, detached from obedient allegiance, are a cymbal — sound with nothing inside.

Jesus ran the same audit on the same inventory, and passed the same sentence: __“have we not *prophesied* in thy name?… and in thy name done many *powers*?”__ — __“depart from me, ye that *work lawlessness*”__ (Matthew 7:22-23).
They plead *powers*; the sentence answers *works*.
Paul names the missing allegiance; Jesus names its lawless fruit.
The terms are not synonyms, but the audit reaches the same defect: a life full of religious gifts while refusing the command.

Samuel passed the sentence first: Saul spared the best of the flock *to sacrifice it* — an offering in place of the command — and heard, __“to *obey* is better than *sacrifice*, and to hearken than the fat of rams”__ (1 Samuel 15:22).
Sacrifice, powers, gifts — the offering never outranks the command.

The catalog that follows is the law in motion.
__“Love *does not envy*”__ — the tenth commandment kept; __“does not seek its own… thinks no *evil*”__ — no ill worked to a neighbor; __“does not rejoice in *lawlessness*, but rejoices in the sym:sym-truth[truth]”__ — and __“thy *law* is the truth”__ (Psalm 119:142).
Paul is not decorating; he is itemizing: __“Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the *fulfilling of the law*”__ (Romans 13:10) — and __“the *purpose of the commandment* is love from a pure heart”__ (1 Timothy 1:5, NKJV).
The commandment's own goal is love; love's own shape is the commandments.

The hymn then turns prophetic:

[quote.scripture, 1 Corinthians 13:8, 10, 12, NKJV]
____
Love *never ends*. But whether there are prophecies, they will end; whether there are tongues, they will cease; whether there is knowledge, it will vanish away…
But when *that which is perfect* has come, then that which is in part will be done away…
For now we see *in a mirror, dimly*, but then *face to face*. Now I sym:sym-knowing[know] in part, but then I shall know just as I also am sym:sym-knowing[*known*].
____

James supplies the mirror: the hearer who is not a doer is __“a man observing his natural face *in a mirror*”__ — and the doer looks __“into the *perfect law* of sym:sym-liberty[liberty]”__ (James 1:23-25).
The mirror we see dimly in is the law; what it shows a man is his own face.
Now the reflection is dim and partial; the day the *perfect* comes, the mediated image gives way to __“face to face”__ — the phrase of Moses, with whom God spoke __“face to face, even plainly, and not in *riddles*”__ (Num 12:8).
Mark where the hymn lands: __“I shall *know* just as I also am *known*”__ — Paul's love chapter ends in the covenant word this chapter defines next.
The gifts are scaffolding and come down; love — covenant allegiance embodied in the commandments — __“never ends,”__ because the law it fulfills does not pass away.

[discrete]
=== Hate

Love has an opposite, and Scripture defines hate with the same precision — not a hotter feeling, but the other pole of the same axis.
Jacob served for two sisters, and the record grades the marriage in consecutive verses: __“he *loved* also Rachel *more than* Leah”__ (Genesis 29:30) — then, one verse later, __“when the LORD saw that Leah was *hated*, he opened her womb”__ (Genesis 29:31).
Leah is a wife in the house, bearing son after son; the hated one is the loved-less, the not-chosen-first — Scripture's own equation, stated where the word first touches a family.
The Gospel translates its own idiom the same way: Luke's __“If any man come to me, and *hate not* his father, and mother… he cannot be my disciple”__ (Luke 14:26) stands in Matthew as __“He that *loveth* father or mother *more than me* is not worthy of me”__ (Matthew 10:37).
To hate is to un-choose — a prior claim renounced.
Wisdom states it as a plain parallel: they __“*hated* knowledge, and *did not choose* the sym:sym-fear[fear of the LORD]”__ (Proverbs 1:29).

When God Himself hates, the grammar is divorce:

[quote.scripture, Hosea 9:15]
____
All their wickedness is in Gilgal: for there I *hated* them: for the wickedness of their doings I will *drive them out of mine house*, I will *love them no more*: all their princes are revolters.
____

Hated, driven out of the house, loved no more — the covenant repudiated step by step, in its own legal order.
The KJV itself knows the word is a standing and not a temperature: six times it renders the Hebrew's _one who hates_ as __“enemies,”__ __“enemy,”__ or __“foes”__ — __“the kisses of an *enemy* are deceitful”__ (Proverbs 27:6) is, in the Hebrew, the kisses of the hater.
Even where the KJV keeps __“hate,”__ the English has drifted underneath it: the translators' word could mean no more than _strongly dislike, reject_, and four centuries have hardened it into hot hostility and little else.
The heat a modern reader feels in these verses is an import the translators never wrote — the word must be read with the Bible's own sense, not our century's.

Where did the feelings go? Scripture keeps them in other words.
Esau's murderous grudge — __“Esau *hated* Jacob… then will I *slay* my brother”__ (Genesis 27:41) — is _satam_, the seething grudge that plots blood; God's __“Esau have I hated”__ (Malachi 1:3) is _sane_, the un-choosing of a line — the KJV's single __“hated”__ hides the two words.
Leviticus splits them in consecutive verses: __“thou shalt not *hate* thy brother in thine heart: thou shalt in any wise *rebuke* thy neighbour”__ (Leviticus 19:17) — the alternative the verse offers to heart-hate is not a warmer feeling but the spoken rebuke, for the brother left unrebuked in his sin is the brother quietly un-chosen — and the grudge follows in the next verse under its own word: __“thou shalt not avenge, *nor bear any grudge*”__ (Leviticus 19:18, _natar_).

So the axis stands whole: love keeps the covenant; hate is the covenant refused — __“them that *hate* me”__ set against __“them that *love* me, and *keep my commandments*”__ (Exodus 20:5-6) — one axis, both enacted, neither an emotional temperature.

[discrete]
=== Knowing

To _know_ God, we assume, is to know about Him — facts, doctrine, a sound creed.
But Jesus turns away people whose facts are exactly right:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 7:23]
____
And then will I profess unto them, *I never knew you*: depart from me, ye that *work lawlessness*.
____

He does not say _you never knew me_; He says _I never knew you_ — and the disqualifier is *lawlessness*.
The Greek is _anomia_ — without _nomos_, without *law* — the word the KJV renders __“iniquity,”__ and the word John uses when he defines sin: __“sin is the *transgression of the law*”__ (1 John 3:4).
Read __“iniquity”__ in the New Testament and this is usually the word underneath — law-breaking, wearing a vaguer name.
To be unknown by God is to be what Scripture calls the one not known — a sym:sym-stranger[stranger]; so the whole sentence reads __“I never knew you: depart from me”__ — put out of the household like a man who was never of it.

John gives the test plainly:

[quote.scripture, 1 John 2:3-4]
____
And hereby we do know that we *know him, if we keep his commandments*.
He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a *liar*, and the sym:sym-truth[truth] is not in him.
____

To know God is a covenant bond proven by obedience — the same sense in which God says of Israel, __“You only have I known of all the families of the earth”__ (Amos 3:2).
Knowing is not information held; it is a relationship kept.

Paul says it with a knife: __“They profess that they *know God*; but in *works* they *deny him*”__ (Titus 1:16).
Hosea mourns the same equation from the ruins: __“My people are destroyed for *lack of knowledge*… seeing thou hast *forgotten the law* of thy God”__ (Hosea 4:6) — the knowledge lost was not information; it was the law.
God defines the knowing by a king’s life: he __“sym:sym-judgment[judged] the cause of the sym:sym-poor[poor] and needy… *was not this to know me?* saith the LORD”__ (Jeremiah 22:16).

The relationship it names runs deeper than acquaintance.
The first time Scripture uses the word of two persons it means the union of marriage — __“Adam *knew* Eve his wife; and she *conceived*”__ (Genesis 4:1) — the union that bears sym:sym-fruit[fruit].
To _know_, at root, is the intimate joining of husband and wife; which is why God calls His covenant a sym:sym-marriage[marriage] and His people a bride.

To know God is to be joined to Him as a wife to her husband — and that union keeps an order: __“the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church”__ (Ephesians 5:23), the bride subject to her Head __“in every thing”__ (Ephesians 5:24).
So the intimacy and the obedience are not two things: to know Him is to be His, and to be His is to obey the Head.
The ones He never knew were never joined to Him — they said __“Lord”__ but were no bride of His.

Put the symbols together and the Shepherd says it whole. __“My sym:sym-sheep[sheep] hear my sym:sym-voice[voice]… and they follow me”__ (John 10:27): the sheep are His people, the voice is His words, and to know that voice is to follow it.
And they follow no other — __“a sym:sym-stranger[stranger] will they not follow… for they know not the sym:sym-voice[voice] of strangers”__ (John 10:5): the stranger is the one outside the covenant, so His sheep will not heed the voice, the teaching, of those outside it. __“He calleth his own sym:sym-sheep[sheep] by sym:sym-name[name]”__ (John 10:3) — and the sym:sym-name[name] is a symbol with its own chapter just ahead.
To the one who overcomes He gives __“a sym:sym-new[new] sym:sym-name[name] written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it”__ (Revelation 2:17) — _known_ only by the one who receives and keeps it.
Sheep, voice, name, stranger, knowing: each word in its place, and not one of them a thing held only in the head.

[discrete]
=== Faith

Belief and faith are not two disconnected substances.
The Greek keeps them in one word-family: _pisteuō_ is to believe; _pistis_ is faith.
Ephesians gives the order: __“after that ye heard the word of truth… after that ye believed”__ (Ephesians 1:13), and Paul concludes, __“faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God”__ (Romans 10:17).
The word is heard; belief receives it as governing truth; hope lays hold of its unseen promise; faith holds that belief steady through delay and testing; works enact it in the life.
Belief can stop at factual assent, as the demons and fearful rulers show.
Living faith cannot exist without belief, and faith without works is dead.

Faith, we are taught, is the one thing that needs no works.
James answers head-on:

[quote.scripture, James 2:17]
____
Even so faith, if it hath not works, is *dead*, being alone.
____

He presses it: __“the devils also believe, and tremble”__ (James 2:19) — perfect assent, and it saves none of them.
The faith Scripture honors always moves: __“By faith Abraham… obeyed”__ (Hebrews 11:8).

The Hebrew behind _faith_ is _emunah_, faithfulness — steadiness, reliability — so __“the just shall live by his faith”__ (Habakkuk 2:4) is to live by one’s faithfulness.
The word’s first appearance in Scripture is a picture: Moses’ hands, held up over the battle, __“were *steady*”__ — _emunah_ — __“until the going down of the sun”__ (Exodus 17:12): faithfulness is hands that do not drop.
Faith is not a conviction lodged in the mind; it is trusting faithfulness — reliance on God's promise held steady through obedience.
The trust and the works are distinguishable, but living faith will not leave them separated.
James says Abraham's faith __“wrought with his works”__ and __“by works was faith made perfect”__ (James 2:22): the works do not rename faith; they enact it and bring it to its goal.

Hebrews states the office in one verse:

[quote.scripture, Hebrews 11:1]
____
Now faith is the *substance* of things *hoped for*, the *evidence* of things *not seen*.
____

Evidence is a thing produced and examined — the unseen promise is proved in the life by the faithfulness it produces.
Scripture keeps the pattern consistently: hope's object is unseen by definition — __“hope that is *seen* is not hope… but if we hope for that we see not, then do we with *patience* wait for it”__ (Romans 8:24-25) — and the patience is faithfulness holding while the thing stays out of sight.
The unseen things are the eternal ones (2 Corinthians 4:18), and __“we *walk* by faith, not by sight”__ (2 Corinthians 5:7): conduct stands in where sight is denied.

Hebrews 11 itself is a catalog of visible acts — Noah, __“warned of God of things *not seen as yet*… prepared an ark”__ (Hebrews 11:7): unseen warning, visible obedience.
What is hoped for, Scripture also names: the resurrection (Acts 24:15), eternal life __“*promised* before the world began”__ (Titus 1:2), the city and better country Abraham looked for (Hebrews 11:10, 16), His appearing (Titus 2:13).
Faith is the trusting fidelity that holds obedience while the promise is still out of sight — a life that can be seen (Matthew 5:16), held steady for things that cannot.

This is not works offered as the purchase price of the promise.
Paul defines that error before he excludes it: __“to him that *worketh* is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of *debt*”__ — then sets over against the wage-claim the man who __“believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly”__ (Romans 4:4-5).
Romans is not setting faith against obedience; it is setting faith against labor offered for a wage.
Jesus makes the distinction exact: __“when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do”__ (Luke 17:10).
Even complete obedience leaves the Master owing no wages.
Ephesians keeps the same order: salvation is __“by grace… through faith… not of works,”__ and those so saved are immediately __“created in Christ Jesus *unto good works*”__ (Ephesians 2:8-10).
The works neither buy the gift nor put God in debt; they are the life the received gift creates.
Faith receives the promise, then remains faithful to the One who promised.

What, then, are the works, without which faith is dead?
Scripture defines the word where the law is first taught: Jethro counsels Moses to __“teach them *ordinances and laws*, and shalt shew them the way wherein they must walk, and *the work that they must do*”__ (Exodus 18:20).
Ordinances taught, a way walked, *the* work done — a work is a deed, not a synonym for obedience.
A work becomes obedience when it executes a legitimate command; it becomes disobedience when the command or deed conflicts with God's command.
Romans 4 speaks of a laborer's work presented for wages; James 2 speaks of Abraham's work as the visible enactment of faith.
The word names the deed; the context names its master and whether any wage is claimed.
Paul's distinct uses of _law_, _works_, _obedience_, _wages_, and _duty_ are traced occurrence by occurrence in link:/books/symbolic-language/the-end-of-the-law/[The End of the Law].
The psalmist holds God's works and God's commandments as the two halves of one line: __“the *works* of his hands are verity and judgment; all his *commandments* are sure”__ (Psalm 111:7).
Jesus holds His works with the commandment-keeping verb: __“he that overcometh, and *keepeth my works* unto the end”__ (Revelation 2:26) — works can be *kept* because works are commandment-shaped.
So the sentence James wrote completes itself: faith without works is dead because works are the commandment-shaped enactment of trust — the keeping this chapter has been proving — and a faith that never acts never becomes faithfulness.

[discrete]
=== Belief

Which leaves _believe_, the word on which whole systems are built — and here the ground is already broken: the link:/books/symbolic-language/gospel/[Gospel] chapter caught Paul trading __“obeyed”__ for __“believed”__ in a single breath (Romans 10:16), and pointed at the Greek of John 3:36.
Now read that famous verse whole:

[quote.scripture, John 3:36, ASV]
____
He that *believeth* on the Son hath eternal sym:sym-life[life]; but he that *obeyeth not* the Son shall not see life…
____

In the covenant question John is asking, the opposite of believing is disobeying.
Receiving the Son's word as governing truth means submitting to the Son who spoke it; persistent refusal to obey exposes the claim of belief as empty.

That does not mean Scripture never uses _believe_ for accepting a fact.
James says __“the devils also *believe*, and tremble”__ (James 2:19), and the Gospels say those same spirits know who Christ is and obey when His authority commands them: __“he commandeth even the unclean spirits, and *they do obey him*”__ (Mark 1:27).
Their belief is real enough to produce trembling and compelled compliance; it is not love, covenant allegiance, or saving trust.
John records the human counterpart: many rulers __“believed on him,”__ but would not confess Him because __“they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God”__ (John 12:42-43).
A man may believe a fact and still act against it because another love, fear, or appetite governs him.

Saving belief is therefore not bare assent and not obedience renamed.
It is receiving God's testimony as governing truth in a response that submits to it.
Where that submission is persistently refused, Scripture judges the claimed belief by its fruit and calls the condition unbelief.

Scripture keeps the pair together: Israel could not enter the land for __“unbelief”__ — they __“believed not”__ — and the refusal that exposed their distrust was disobedience (Hebrews 3:18-19).
Abraham, who __“believed in the LORD”__ (Genesis 15:6), is later shown to have been __“justified by works, when he had offered Isaac”__ (James 2:21): the obedience did not replace his belief; it brought the belief to its declared end, __“and by works was faith made perfect”__ (James 2:22).

The four words converge, then, in one covenant response — and keep four distinct offices.
*Love* is self-giving covenant allegiance embodied, for us, in the keeping: __“this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments”__ (1 John 5:3).
*Faith* keeps them in hope of the promise — __“faith is the substance of things *hoped for*”__ (Heb 11:1); Abraham __“obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went… for he looked for a city”__ (Heb 11:8-10).
*Belief* receives the word as governing sym:sym-truth[truth] and submits to it: Thomas believed __“because thou hast seen”__ — and the Lord blessed __“they that have not seen, and yet have believed”__ (John 20:29), grading the two grounds in a single sentence.

*Knowing* keeps them as a bride keeps covenant — __“I will betroth thee unto me in *faithfulness*: and thou shalt *know* the LORD”__ (Hos 2:20); __“He judged the cause of the poor and needy… was not this to know me?”__ (Jer 22:16).
One covenant response, four distinguishable offices — and *faithful* is Scripture's word for that allegiance kept *consistent*: Moses' hands __“steady until the going down of the sun”__ (Ex 17:12), the servant found __“so doing”__ when his lord comes (Matt 24:46), __“faithful unto death”__ (Rev 2:10).
Flatten them into synonyms and each goes invisible — which is what the dictionary did, so a man could claim all four and live as he pleased.
Scripture binds them back together and sets them where they can be seen — in a life that does what God said.

See, then, what the symbols do to the simplest promise of all.

[quote.scripture, Romans 10:13]
____
For whosoever shall *call upon* the sym:sym-name[name] of the Lord shall be *saved*.
____

It is heard as a sentence you say — profess the name, and salvation is done.
Then remember the many this chapter has already met — who prophesied and did wonders *in that name*, and were not known.
They said the name; whatever it is to _call upon_ it, they did not do it.
So what *is* the sym:sym-name[name], that calling upon it saves and merely saying it does not?
The question has a chapter of its own just ahead — link:/books/symbolic-language/the-name/[The Name] — and everything this chapter proved about knowing, loving, and obeying rides on its answer.

This is what knowing the symbolic language does, and why it changes everything: the verse you thought you had mastered turns out to ask for your whole life.

---
title: "The Way, The Truth, and The Life"
slug: the-way-the-truth-and-the-life
order: 7
permalink: /books/symbolic-language/the-way-the-truth-and-the-life/
description: "Jesus' most-quoted line is three defined symbols in one: THE way is covenant-conduct, THE truth is God's law-standard, THE life is covenant-existence. Together they are the Torah — and the One who speaks them is the law embodied: the Gospel chapter's claim said now in the first person."
og_title: "The Way, The Truth, and The Life — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "…ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls."
    ref: "Jeremiah 6:16"
---
Few verses are quoted more often, or examined less, than the one in which Jesus gathers three of His titles into a single breath:

[quote.scripture, John 14:6]
____
Jesus saith unto him, I am *the way*, *the truth*, and *the life*: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
____

We hear it as one claim — Jesus is the only road to heaven — and move on.
But He has named _three_ things, not one, each a word Scripture has already filled with meaning; and the small word fastened to each is _the_ — not _a_ way, _a_ truth, _a_ life, but _the_, the particular one God defines.

Note, too, where the road actually leads: He says __“unto the Father,”__ not __“to heaven.”__
In Scripture the hope was never to climb up to sym:sym-heaven[heaven] but for heaven to come down to earth — the holy city descending, God dwelling with men (Revelation 21:2-3).
Take the three in the order He gave them.

[discrete]
=== The Way

Begin with __“the way.”__
The Hebrew for a way, _derek_, comes from a verb meaning to tread: a road is not laid down before anyone walks it; it is _made_ by the walking.
So a person’s __“way”__ is not where they are headed but _how they go_ — their conduct, their manner of life.
Scripture defines __“the way of the LORD”__ the first time the phrase appears:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 18:19]
____
…they shall keep *the way of the LORD*, to do sym:sym-justice[justice] and sym:sym-judgment[judgment]…
____

Not a feeling, not a direction — a manner of living: __“to do justice and judgment.”__
Covenant-conduct, measured by God’s standard.
Peter says the same from the other side, laying __“the way of sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness]”__ alongside __“the holy commandment”__ (2 Peter 2:21) — one thing named twice.
This is the way Jesus sets against its opposite:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 7:13-14]
____
…wide is the sym:sym-door[gate], and broad is *the way*, that leadeth to *destruction*… narrow is *the way*, which *leadeth unto life*, and few there be that find it.
____

Two ways, two manners of walking, two ends.
The narrow way is no secret route; it is the disciplined, Torah-shaped conduct that leads to life.
Which is why the first followers of Jesus were not called Christians but were known, simply, as __“the Way”__ — and when Paul was charged with belonging to it, here is how he owned the name:

[quote.scripture, Acts 24:14]
____
…after *the way* which they call heresy, so sym:sym-worship[worship] I the God of my fathers, sym:sym-belief[believing] *all things which are written in the law and in the prophets*.
____

__“The Way”__ was not a new religion.
It was the old covenant-conduct — __“believing all things which are written in the law and in the prophets”__ — now walked in the light of its Messiah.

[discrete]
=== The Truth

Next, __“the truth.”__
Here too the modern ear hears the wrong thing: we take truth to mean factual accuracy, a statement that matches the world.
But Scripture says plainly what _the_ truth is:

[quote.scripture, Psalm 119:142]
____
Thy sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness] is an everlasting righteousness, and thy *law* is *the truth*.
____

Not __“thy law is true,”__ but __“thy law _is_ the truth”__ — the standard itself, the measure by which everything else is weighed.
Jesus prays it the same way:

[quote.scripture, John 17:17]
____
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy *word* is *truth*.
____

The law, the word — the covenant standard — _is_ the truth.
Other things are true only as they answer to it.
So __“the truth”__ is not a heap of correct facts; it is God’s own measure, His commandments, His word.

[discrete]
=== The Life

Third, __“the life.”__
The word covers every breathing thing, but _the_ life is narrower — the covenant-existence that flows from God and defines His people.
John opens his Gospel by setting it equal to another symbol:

[quote.scripture, John 1:4]
____
In him was life; and *the life* was the sym:sym-light[light] of men.
____

The life _was_ the light — and light is a defined symbol with link:/books/symbolic-language/light-and-darkness/[its own chapter ahead]: not truth in the abstract, but the law lived where men can see it (Matthew 5:16).footnote:fn07light516[Derived in the link:/books/symbolic-language/light-and-darkness/[Light and Darkness] chapter.]
So John’s equation compounds the symbols: the covenant-existence, held perfectly in Him, was itself the lived example — obedience demonstrated in the open, where men could watch it and walk by it.
The life does not merely exist; it shows.

The law itself is called by this name:

[quote.scripture, Proverbs 3:18]
____
She is a sym:sym-tree[tree] of sym:sym-life[life] to them that lay hold upon her: and happy is every one that retaineth her.
____

Two symbols compound in that phrase: the tree is a nation, and the life is the covenant-existence just defined — so the tree of life is the living nation, the community whose obedience is on display; and what one lays hold of to belong to it is sym:sym-wisdom[wisdom], link:/books/symbolic-language/the-fool-and-the-wise/[the law kept and done] (Deuteronomy 4:6).footnote:fn07deut46[Derived in the chapter link:/books/symbolic-language/the-fool-and-the-wise/[The Fool and the Wise].]
(The tree as a symbol of the nation is its own study; here it is enough that the law and the life are bound together.)

This is why the narrow _way_ __“leadeth unto life”__ (Matthew 7:14): the conduct yields the existence.
Walk the pattern, and you enter the life it produces.

[discrete]
=== The Highway

There is a companion to __“the way”__ that English blurs into it.
A way (_derek_) is _how_ you walk — conduct.
A _highway_ (_mesillah_, from a root meaning to _cast up_, to raise) is _where_ you walk — the road itself, built up above the wilderness, cleared of stones, public and unmistakable.
Isaiah names them in one breath:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 35:8-9]
____
And an sym:sym-highway[highway] shall be there, and a *way*, and it shall be called *The way of holiness*; the unclean shall not pass over it; but it shall be for those: the wayfaring men, though sym:sym-fool[fools], shall not err therein.
No sym:sym-lion[lion] shall be there, nor any ravenous sym:sym-beast[beast] shall go up thereon, it shall not be found there; but *the redeemed shall walk there*.
____

The highway is the covenant road — raised, holy, and safe — and every clause of the promise is built of symbols we can now read.
No lion, no ravenous beast: the beast is a defined symbol — a kingdom of the world, __“the fourth sym:sym-beast[beast] shall be the fourth *kingdom* upon earth”__ (Daniel 7:23) — and the lion is the beast Scripture names a ruler: __“As a roaring sym:sym-lion[lion]… so is a *wicked ruler* over the poor people”__ (Proverbs 28:15); __“her *princes* within her are roaring lions”__ (Zephaniah 3:3); __“Israel is a scattered sym:sym-sheep[sheep]; the *lions* have driven him away: first the *king of Assyria*… and last this *Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon*”__ (Jeremiah 50:17).
On every other road the flock walks hunted — the empires roar like lions and __“lay hold of the prey… and none shall deliver”__ (Isaiah 5:29) — but no devouring ruler can set foot on this one, and the scattered sheep walk home unhunted: __“they shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy sym:sym-mountain[mountain]”__ (Isaiah 11:9).

Even the sym:sym-fool[fool] — the man who hears God’s word and will not do it — __“shall not err therein”__: the covenant road is so plainly built that finding it was never the fool’s problem; __“it is *not hidden* from thee, neither is it far off… the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest *do it*”__ (Deuteronomy 30:11, 14).
It must be _prepared_: __“make straight in the desert a highway for our God”__ (Isaiah 40:3) — not a work of shovels but of repentance, the cry John the Baptist took up, clearing the obstacles off the covenant road.
Where a people break the covenant, the road falls empty: __“the highways lie waste… he hath broken the covenant”__ (Isaiah 33:8).

It is the road in Jesus’ parable of the wedding feast.
When those first bidden refuse, the king does not cancel the feast — he widens the summons:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 22:9-10]
____
Go ye therefore into the sym:sym-highway[highways], and as many as ye shall find, *bid to the* sym:sym-marriage[marriage]… and the wedding was *furnished with guests*.
____

The call goes out to the highways and the house is filled — __“compel them to come in, that my house may be filled”__ (Luke 14:23).
Yet one guest is found there __“which had not on a wedding sym:sym-garment[garment]”__ (Matthew 22:11), and is cast out: to be _on_ the highway is not enough; the _way_ — the conduct, the garment one wears — must match the road.
Where and how stand or fall together, which is just what Isaiah called them: __“the way of holiness.”__

[discrete]
=== The Door

Where does the road lead?
To a door.
The highway of holiness runs home to the house of God, and the entrance is a person:

[quote.scripture, John 10:9]
____
I am *the door*: by me if any man *enter in*, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture.
____

Not a door among doors — _the_ door, the one way in.
Now see what Scripture marks a doorway with.
On its posts is _written_ the word of God: __“thou shalt write them upon the door posts of thine house, and upon thy gates”__ (Deuteronomy 11:20) — the commandments, the law, _the truth_, inscribed on the very frame you pass through.
And on its posts is _spread_ the blood of the sym:sym-lamb[lamb]:

[quote.scripture, Exodus 12:13]
____
And the *blood* shall be to you for a token upon the houses… and when I see the *blood*, I will pass over you, and the plague shall not be upon you to destroy you.
____

The doorway of God’s house bears the _word_ on its posts and the _blood_ on its posts — the law and the lamb, the truth and the cross.
Christ is that door.
To come in by Him is to come in by the word and by the blood: past the commandment that is the truth, under the blood that turns the destroyer away.

[discrete]
=== One Torah, Three Aspects

Set the three side by side and they are not separate claims but one reality seen from three angles.
Solomon had already strung them on a single thread:

[quote.scripture, Proverbs 6:23]
____
For the *commandment* is a sym:sym-lamp[lamp]; and the *law* is sym:sym-light[light]; and reproofs of sym:sym-instruction[instruction] are the *way of life*.
____

The commandment — the standard, __“the truth”__ — made visible as light, becomes a __“way of life”__: conduct that yields existence.
The truth defines the way; the way produces the life.
One Torah, three aspects: the measure, the walking, and the living.

From the gate of Eden the whole of it was already in view.
There a __“flaming sym:sym-sword[sword]”__ was set __“to keep the way of the sym:sym-tree[tree] of sym:sym-life[life]”__ (Genesis 3:24).
The word rendered __“keep”__ is _shamar_ — to guard, to protect, to keep, to preserve and maintain; the very charge first given to Adam, to __“keep”__ the garden (Genesis 2:15).
It does not mean to _bar_ the way but to _preserve_ it.

What is that flaming sword?
Paul names it: __“the sym:sym-sword[sword] of the Spirit, which is the word of God”__ (Ephesians 6:17) — the same word Hebrews calls __“sharper than any twoedged sym:sym-sword[sword]”__ (Hebrews 4:12).
So from the very beginning the _word of God_ has stood guard over the way of life — the truth guarding the way to the life, the three already bound together and kept open by the Word that runs through them all.
(The sword and the flame are each their own study; here it is enough to see the Word keeping the way.)

[discrete]
=== The Torah Embodied

Now return to where we began, and the three titles open.
When Jesus says __“I am the way, the truth, and the life,”__ He is not stacking three metaphors.
He is saying that the whole of it — the standard, the conduct, the existence — has become a person.

He _is_ __“the truth”__: the law in the flesh, the commandment no longer cut in stone or even written on the heart but _living_, speaking, demonstrating.
He _is_ __“the way”__: covenant-conduct walked, for once, perfectly — the road made by His own treading.
Hebrews names that road with a word every major translation flattens to __“new”__:

[quote.scripture, Hebrews 10:19-20]
____
Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, By a *freshly-slain and living way*, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, *his flesh*;
____

The Greek behind the usual __“new”__ is _prosphatos_ — built on the verb for slaughter: freshly slain.footnote:heb1020[_Prosphatos_ (Hebrews 10:20), from _pro_ + _sphazō_, “to slaughter” — literally “freshly slaughtered”; every major translation renders it “new.”
The word-by-word study is at https://TimeTested.Bible[TimeTested.Bible].]
A way freshly slain and living at once — the same paradox handed to every disciple who walks it: __“present your bodies a *living sacrifice*”__ (Romans 12:1).
The road into the holiest is a Person freshly slain and alive forevermore, consecrated for us through the veil of His own flesh.
And He _is_ __“the life”__: the covenant-existence the way leads to, held so fully that death could not keep it —

[quote.scripture, John 11:25]
____
…I am the resurrection, and *the life*: he that sym:sym-belief[believeth] in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live.
____

This is the same claim the Gospel chapter made about the **gospel**footnote:gospel[_Gospel_ — the message Jesus taught, not the message about Him; see the link:/books/symbolic-language/gospel/[Gospel] chapter.] — the law of the kingdom, the renewed covenant written on the heart — said now in the first person.
The One who _is_ that law, kept whole in a single human life, can say without exaggeration: __“I am the way, the truth, and the life.”__
He is the Torah embodied — the standard walking.

The last line, then, is not the slammed door it is so often made to sound: __“no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.”__
Read through the symbols, it is simply this: there has only ever been _one_ way — one covenant-conduct, one standard, one life — and it now has a name.
Not a new road to God, but the original road, walked perfectly and thrown open.
To come by Him is to walk the way He is, by the truth He is, through the door He is, into the life He is.

The sym:sym-name[name] He bears — what it is in this symbolic language, what it carries, and why everything hangs on it — is the next chapter.

---
title: "The Name"
slug: the-name
order: 8
permalink: /books/symbolic-language/the-name/
description: "Almost everyone thinks 'taking the name in vain' is about cursing or mispronouncing YHWH, and that 'in Jesus' name' is a phrase that makes prayers work. Both treat the name as a sound. Scripture builds a different answer: the name is the covenant — borne by obedience, kept by the law, owned as a bride takes a husband's. To be called by His name is to come under His wing, whose corners carry the reminder of the commandments; Babel's counterfeit is the name self-made — and most who say 'Lord, Lord' take it in vain."
og_title: "The Name — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe."
    ref: "Proverbs 18:10"
---
Two things almost everyone believes about __“the name”__ turn out to be wrong, and they are the two doors most people walk in by.
The first: that to __“take the LORD’s name in vain”__ is to curse — __“oh my God”__ as an idle breath — or to mangle the sacred syllables, YHWH, Yahweh, Yahuah.
The second is quieter.
We end our prayers __“in Jesus’ name,”__ as though the phrase were a key that turns the lock — and when nothing turns, we quietly wonder what went wrong.

Both mistakes treat the name as a _sound_: a word to pronounce correctly, or a formula to attach.
But Jesus made a promise about His name that no magic word could keep:

[quote.scripture, John 14:13]
____
And *whatsoever ye shall ask in my name*, that will I do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son.
____

_Whatsoever_ — and yet how many prayers, sealed with the name, go unanswered?
Either the promise fails, or __“in my name”__ means something deeper than a phrase we append.
To find it we must stop asking how the name _sounds_ and ask what it _is_ — and Scripture builds the answer a piece at a time.

[discrete]
=== In My Name

Begin with that promise.
To ask __“in my name”__ is not to invoke a syllable but to ask _as one who belongs to Him_ — within His will, on His terms, inside the relationship.
Paul says the same of the whole of life: __“whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus”__ (Colossians 3:17).
You cannot do _everything_ by pronouncing a word over it; you can only do everything _within a relationship_.
To act __“in the name”__ is to act inside the bond.

The bond is something a person _carries_.
At Sinai, God named the guide who went before His people — one with the name itself _in him_:

[quote.scripture, Exodus 23:20-21]
____
Behold, I send an Angel before thee, to *keep thee in the* sym:sym-way[way], and to bring thee into *the place which I have prepared*… Beware of him, and obey his sym:sym-voice[voice], provoke him not; for he will not pardon your transgressions: for *my name is in him*.
____

This is no created messenger.
He bears God’s own _name_ — His presence and authority — and Scripture, looking back, tells us plainly who he was: __“the angel of his presence saved them… and he bare them, and carried them all the days of old”__ (Isaiah 63:9).
The sym:sym-rock[Rock] that followed Israel through the wilderness, Paul says, __“was Christ”__ (1 Corinthians 10:4).
So Christ — the One in whom the name dwelt — led them by the pillar of cloud and fire; and the same One came in the flesh.
(One clause does reach ahead: this Angel __“will not pardon your transgressions”__ — and transgress they did, at the very foot of the mountain; the name-bearer who would at last _pardon_ comes only when He takes flesh.)

When Jesus says __“I have declared unto them thy name”__ (John 17:26), He is not reciting a sound He learned; He is that name-bearer, now walking among His people — the name _borne_ in a person, made visible in a faithful life, and kept the way it always was: He keeps them __“in the sym:sym-way[way]”__ (covenant-conduct); they must __“obey his voice.”__

The promise looked beyond that generation’s journey.
The Angel was sent __“to bring thee into the place which I have prepared”__ — the very words the name-bearer would take up as His own: __“I go to prepare a place for you… I will come again, and receive you unto myself”__ (John 14:2-3).
The One in whom the name dwells led Israel through the wilderness, came in the flesh, and will come again to gather His people into the place He has prepared — one name-bearer, from the wilderness to the end.

[discrete]
=== Lord, Lord

Which sets up the sharpest test Jesus ever gave.
Picture the people most certain of their standing:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 7:22-23]
____
Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy *name*? and in thy *name* have cast out devils? and in thy *name* done many *powers*?footnote:dynameis[The King James prints “wonderful works”; the Greek is _dynameis_ — powers, not _erga_, works.]
And then will I profess unto them, *I never* sym:sym-knowing[knew] *you*: depart from me, ye that *work lawlessness*.
____

Every sentence has the name in it — prophesying, casting out devils, doing powers __“in thy name.”__
No one ever spoke it more.
He turns them away as __“workers of *lawlessness*”__ — _anomia_.
They had the sound and not the substance.

The name cannot be a word on the lips: a man may have it there constantly and remain a stranger to the One who bears it.
What, then, _is_ it?

[discrete]
=== The Name Is the Covenant

Here at last Scripture says it outright.
David, settled in his palace, wants to build a house for the _ark of the covenant_:

[quote.scripture, 2 Samuel 7:2]
____
…I dwell in an house of cedar, but the *ark of God* dwelleth within curtains.
____

God answers, and quietly trades one word for another:

[quote.scripture, 2 Samuel 7:13]
____
He shall build an house for my *name*, and I will stablish the throne of his kingdom for ever.
____

David said _the ark of the covenant_; God said _my name_.
They are the same thing.
The name _is_ the **covenant**footnote:covenant[_Covenant_ — the renewed covenant of the kingdom; see the link:/books/symbolic-language/gospel/[Gospel] chapter.] — the binding relationship between God and His people.

Notice that God, answering, plays on David’s own word — for a __“house”__ in Scripture is a building _and_ a family line, and a family line is exactly what carries a name.
David offered to build God a house of stone; God replies, __“the LORD telleth thee that *he will make thee an house*”__ (2 Samuel 7:11) — not cedar but sons: the house _of David_.

The promise then stands established three ways at once, and every level holds.
In the flesh: the seed and throne endure — __“the Lord God shall give unto him the *throne of his father David*… and of his kingdom there shall be *no end*”__ (Luke 1:32-33).
In stone: Solomon raises the temple __“for my name.”__
And in covenant: the Son of David builds the house the first two only sketched — __“Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up… he spake of the *temple of his body*”__ (John 2:19-21); __“ye also, as lively sym:sym-stone[stones], are *built up a spiritual house*”__ (1 Peter 2:5); __“Christ as a son over his own house; *whose house are we*”__ (Hebrews 3:6).

Zechariah compresses the whole promise into one oracle:

[quote.scripture, Zechariah 6:12-13]
____
…Behold the man whose *name* is The BRANCH; and he shall grow up out of his place, and he shall *build the temple* of the LORD:
Even he shall build the temple of the LORD; and he shall bear the glory, and shall sit and *rule upon his throne*; and he shall be a priest upon his throne: and the counsel of peace shall be between them both.
____

Name, house, and throne in one Man.
The wordplay is the doctrine: a house exists to carry a name, and God’s answer to David binds His name and David’s house into a single building.

Now everything before falls into place: this is why asking __“in his name”__ is asking within the covenant; why the name is _borne_ by the obedient; why the man who only _speaks_ it is unknown.
And it is why __“there is none other name under heaven… whereby we must be saved”__ (Acts 4:12): no other name, because no other _covenant_.
To __“sym:sym-belief[believe] on his name”__ (John 1:12) is not to credit a title but to enter that covenant in trusting obedience.

It is also why the name can be a refuge:

[quote.scripture, Proverbs 18:10]
____
The name of the LORD is a *strong tower*: the righteous *runneth into it*, and is safe.
____

No one takes shelter inside a sound.
A covenant can be run into — walls, a roof, and a door that shuts behind the one who keeps it.

It even untangles an old puzzle.
God tells Moses He was __“not known”__ to the patriarchs __“by my name JEHOVAH”__ (Exodus 6:3) — though Abraham plainly _heard_ the word, __“I am the LORD that brought thee out of Ur”__ (Genesis 15:7).
He knew the _sound_; he had not yet entered the _covenant_ that name would come to carry.

Which is exactly why the argument over the right syllables, earnest as it is, looks straight past the thing itself.
The name is not a sound to recover.
It is a covenant to keep.

[discrete]
=== Taking It in Vain

Now — and only now — the commandment opens:

[quote.scripture, Exodus 20:7]
____
Thou shalt not take the *name* of the LORD thy God *in vain*; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his *name* in vain.
____

__“Vain”__ is _shav_ — emptiness, _for nothing_.
To take the name in vain is to take the _covenant_ for nothing: to wear it, claim it, swear by it, while living as though it asks nothing of you.
It was never first a sin of the mouth; it is a sin of the life.
The cursing man breaks it, yes — but so does the one who cries __“Lord, Lord”__ and works lawlessness, and the one who seals empty prayers with a name he will not keep.

Solomon files that exact case:

[quote.scripture, Proverbs 28:9]
____
He that turneth away his ear from *hearing the law*, even his *prayer* shall be *abomination*.
____

The mouth full of the name, the ear turned from the covenant that fills it: such prayer does not merely go unanswered, it offends.
There is the answer to the puzzle this chapter opened with: the prayer sealed __“in the name”__ fails because the ear has left the law.
Most who take His name in vain do it inside the church.

The prophets prosecute the same sin under another verb.
__“When they entered unto the heathen… they *profaned my holy name*, when they said to them, These are *the people of the LORD*, and are gone forth out of his land”__ (Ezekiel 36:20).
Israel did not profane the name by mispronouncing it; they profaned it by wearing it faithlessly in front of the nations — covenant-breakers introduced everywhere as the covenant people.
And God’s remedy is not a correction of speech: __“I will *sanctify my great name*, which was profaned among the heathen… when I shall be *sanctified in you* before their eyes”__ (Ezekiel 36:23) — He hallows His own name by making the people who wear it holy.

[discrete]
=== The Lord’s Prayer

The most familiar prayer in the world asks for exactly this — and once the name is understood, the whole prayer opens, line by line.
Its grammar carries more weight than the recitation lets on.
__“*Hallowed be thy name*”__ (Matthew 6:9) is not a description and not a compliment; the verb is an imperative: _let thy name be made holy_ — the one praying is demanding the very thing Ezekiel promised, that the name be hallowed in its people before the eyes of the world.

Hear the petitions that march out behind it, each in the same commanding mood: __“Thy *kingdom come*.
Thy *will be done* in earth, as it is in heaven”__ (Matthew 6:10).
Name hallowed, kingdom come, will _done_ — the covenant kept holy in a people, the King’s reign arriving, and His will obeyed on earth the way heaven already obeys it.
The second petition tells us how the first is granted: a name is hallowed when the will of its Bearer is done — beginning with the one praying.

The covenant runs through every petition that follows; walk them with the Bible’s symbolic language in hand.
__“Give us this day our daily sym:sym-bread[bread]”__ (Matthew 6:11) — and bread is a defined symbol: the *word* from the mouth of the LORD (Deuteronomy 8:3).
The petition even has a history, for the first daily bread was the manna — rained from heaven one day’s portion at a time, and God states His purpose in the giving: __“that I may *prove* them, whether they will *walk in my law*, or no”__ (Exodus 16:4).

Luke’s wording keeps the manna’s rhythm exactly — __“Give us *day by day* our daily sym:sym-bread[bread]”__ (Luke 11:3) — and when Luke’s Jesus finishes the prayer, He walks straight into a parable of a man begging *three loaves at midnight* and a Father who gives to them that ask (Luke 11:5-13): the petition, dramatized.
To ask for daily bread is to ask for the day’s portion of the word — and to take up the day’s test of walking in it.

__“And forgive us our *debts*, as *we* forgive our debtors”__ (Matthew 6:12).
The release of debts is the law’s own mercy — __“every creditor that lendeth ought unto his neighbour shall *release* it… because it is called *the LORD’S release*”__ (Deuteronomy 15:2) — and the petition asks God to run His release toward us as we run it toward our brothers.
Luke’s version glosses the symbol as it goes: __“And forgive us our sym:sym-sin[sins]; for we also forgive every one that is *indebted* to us”__ (Luke 11:4) — sins in the first clause, debtors in the second: the two gospels set the columns side by side, and the debt is sin.

It is the one line of the prayer Jesus stops to underline the moment He finishes teaching it — __“For *if ye forgive* men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: but *if ye forgive not*…”__ (Matthew 6:14-15) — and He later stages it as a full drama: the servant forgiven ten thousand talents who takes his brother by the throat, and is delivered back to the tormentors (Matthew 18:32-35).
The prayer must be practiced by the man praying it, or it testifies against him.

The last petition asks the covenant God for the covenant deliverance: __“lead us not into temptation, but *deliver us* from evil”__ (Matthew 6:13).
Both halves repay testing.

__“Temptation”__ translates a Greek word that means the _proving_, and James rules out the modern reading in one stroke: __“God cannot be tempted with evil, *neither tempteth he any man*”__ (James 1:13) — yet the same James calls the man blessed who _endures_ it: __“when he is *tried*, he shall receive the *crown of life*”__ (James 1:12).

Beneath the Greek stands a Hebrew word the King James renders both ways, and the wobble is our familiar signpost: __“God did *tempt* Abraham”__ (Genesis 22:1) — the first __“tempt”__ in the Bible, in the very scene that gives us the first __“worship”__ (Genesis 22:5, a discovery the link:/books/symbolic-language/worship/[Worship] chapter will unfold) — is the same word as __“that I may *prove* them”__ over the manna (Exodus 16:4), and __“to *prove* thee… whether thou wouldest *keep his commandments*, or no”__ (Deuteronomy 8:2); David even prays _for_ it: __“*prove* me”__ (Psalm 26:2).
The petition, then, does not imagine God dangling sin; it pleads about the furnace-hour of proving — __“the *hour of temptation*, which shall come upon all the world, to *try* them”__ (Revelation 3:10) — the same plea Jesus pressed on His sleeping disciples in Gethsemane: __“Watch and pray, that ye *enter not into temptation*”__ (Matthew 26:41).

The plea __“deliver us from evil”__ is personal in the Greek — _deliver us from the evil one_: the same __“wicked one”__ who snatches the sown word and fathers the sym:sym-tares[tares] (Matthew 13:19, 38).
Watch the Name-bearer pray this very petition over a man:

[quote.scripture, Luke 22:31-32]
____
…Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as sym:sym-wheat[wheat]:
But *I have prayed for thee*, that thy sym:sym-faith[faith] fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren.
____

Trial itself is not prayed away — the manna was given to prove — the plea is to be brought _through_ the proving and out of the destroyer’s hand, with the promise standing behind it: God __“will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a *way to escape*”__ (1 Corinthians 10:13).

Read whole, the prayer Jesus taught is the covenant renewed in miniature: the name hallowed, the kingdom summoned, the will obeyed, the word received daily, the release practiced, the deliverance promised.
Every line of it is prayed __“in the name,”__ because every line of it lives inside the covenant — and its salvation is promised to those who practice what they pray.

[discrete]
=== Keeping the Name

How, then, is the name kept full rather than emptied?
By its terms — the law.
Moses binds the two in a single line:

[quote.scripture, Deuteronomy 28:58]
____
If thou wilt not observe to do *all the words of this law* that are written in this book, that thou mayest sym:sym-fear[fear] *this glorious and fearful name*, THE LORD THY GOD…
____

Keep the law and you honor the name; despise the law and you empty it.
So at the very end of the story, the people who belong to God are marked by that exact pairing — __“they that keep the commandments of God, and the sym:sym-faith[faith] of Jesus”__ (Revelation 14:12) — with __“his Father’s name written in their foreheads”__ (Revelation 14:1): the covenant owned and worn where all can see — the sym:sym-seal[seal] set on God’s servants.
Scripture binds the name and the law together, and will not let them be pried apart.

[discrete]
=== The Counterfeit Name

In the Bible’s symbolic language, many symbols come paired with an opposite — and describing the opposite often sheds light on the meaning of its counterpart.
The name has such an opposite, and it is the oldest counterfeit on record.

On the plain of Shinar the builders said, __“let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and *let us make us a name*”__ (Genesis 11:4) — sym:sym-babel[Babel], the kingdom whose founding act is a self-made name: an identity manufactured from below, a covenant with no one above.
God’s answer stands in the very next chapter, spoken to one man called out of that world: __“I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and *make thy name great*”__ (Genesis 12:2).
A made name or a given one — the whole war of the Bible in two clauses.

The war ends on men’s foreheads.
The beast __“causeth all… to receive a mark in their right hand, or in their *foreheads*… the *name of the* sym:sym-beast[beast]”__ (Revelation 13:16-17); one chapter later, the Lamb’s company stands on mount Sion __“having his *Father’s name* written in their foreheads”__ (Revelation 14:1).
There is no unmarked forehead in that scene.
Everyone wears a name — the one men make for themselves, or the one God gives — and the commandment asks which one you will refuse to carry for nothing.

[discrete]
=== Called by His Name

One question remains: how does a person come to bear a name that is not his own?
Scripture answers with the oldest institution it has — a bride takes her husband’s — and Isaiah shows the formula in a single desperate verse:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 4:1]
____
And in that day seven women shall take hold of one man, saying, We will eat our own sym:sym-bread[bread], and wear our own sym:sym-garment[apparel]: only *let us be called by thy name*, to take away our *reproach*.
____

To be __“called by thy name”__ is to be sym:sym-marriage[married] — that is the whole request — and the women’s bargain proves it: the law obliges a husband to supply his wife’s __“food, her raiment, and her duty of marriage”__ (Exodus 21:10), and these seven offer to waive everything but the name itself.
Read in the Bible’s symbolic language, the bargain turns chilling.

Seven women — seven, the number Scripture gives the assemblies of God’s people (Revelation 1:20) — asking to wear the Bridegroom’s name while eating _their own_ bread and wearing _their own_ apparel: their own word in place of His, their own righteousness in place of His.
It is the __“Lord, Lord”__ of Matthew 7 spoken as a marriage proposal — the name, minus the covenant that fills it.
And the true Husband gives His sym:sym-widow[widowed] people exactly link:/books/symbolic-language/orphans-widows-and-the-fatherless/[the two things these women decline] — __“food and raiment”__ (Deuteronomy 10:18): the sym:sym-bread[bread] of His word and the sym:sym-garment[garment] of His righteousness.footnote:fn08foodraiment[The food and the raiment are opened fully in the link:/books/symbolic-language/orphans-widows-and-the-fatherless/[Orphans, Widows, and the Fatherless] chapter.]

The true marriage is enacted through the same covenant mechanics.
When Ruth asks Boaz for marriage, she asks him to spread the corner of his garment over her (Ruth 3:9) — and __“skirt”__ there is the Hebrew _kanaph_, the sym:sym-wings[wing]: the covenant edge.

For Ruth is everything the seven women are not, and her story keeps the ledger.
She brings no bread of her own: she eats at Boaz’s table until she __“was sufficed, and *left*”__ (Ruth 2:14), gleans his field by the law of the corner — with __“handfuls *of purpose*”__ dropped in her path (Ruth 2:16) — and is sent home under six measures of barley with the charge, __“Go not *empty*”__ (Ruth 3:17).
And the only raiment the story provides her is the one she asks for.
Boaz had blessed her, __“a full reward be given thee of the LORD God of Israel, under whose sym:sym-wings[wings] thou art come to trust”__ (Ruth 2:12) — and on the threshing floor she asks him to make good his own blessing in person: the widow’s garment laid aside (Ruth 3:3), and one covering requested — his.

God describes His own wedding to Israel with the same gesture:

[quote.scripture, Ezekiel 16:8]
____
Now when I passed by thee, and looked upon thee, behold, thy time was the time of love; and I *spread my skirt* over thee, and covered thy sym:sym-naked[nakedness]: yea, I sware unto thee, and *entered into a covenant* with thee, saith the Lord GOD, and *thou becamest mine*.
____

There the raiment clause is written out in full, in the verses that follow the spread skirt: __“Then washed I thee… I anointed thee… I *clothed thee* also with broidered work… and I covered thee with silk… thy *raiment* was of fine linen… thou didst *eat* fine flour, and honey, and oil”__ (Ezekiel 16:9-13) — food and raiment, both from the Husband, exactly the provision the seven women waived.

To take the husband’s name is to come under the husband’s wing — and the wing’s corners carry the sym:sym-tzitzit[tassels], bound there so that the wearer remembers all the commandments of the LORD and does them (Numbers 15:38-39).
The covering a bride enters when she takes the name is stitched at every corner with the reminder of the law of the One who spreads it — and a bleeding woman once link:/books/symbolic-language/wings/[took hold of that corner] in sym:sym-faith[faith], and the name did what no sound can (Matthew 9:20-21).footnote:fn08wings[The wing, the fringe bound at its corner, and the healing found there are derived in the link:/books/symbolic-language/wings/[Wings] chapter.]
The name and the commandments arrive as one garment — which is why the name is kept by keeping the law (Deuteronomy 28:58), and emptied any other way.

This grasp is the gesture the nations finally learn.
Isaiah’s seven women __“take hold”__ of one man; Zechariah sees the same verb close on the right thing:

[quote.scripture, Zechariah 8:23]
____
…ten men shall *take hold* out of all languages of the nations, even shall take hold of the *skirt* of him that is a Jew, saying, *We will go with you*: for we have heard that *God is with you*.
____

The hand closes on the _kanaph_ — the wing-corner where the commandments hang — and the words are Ruth’s own, the Moabite bride who said __“whither thou goest, I will go”__ (Ruth 1:16).

Ruth’s wedding under the wing leads directly into this chapter’s closing point.
The law states the purpose of a kinsman’s marriage in name-language: the son is raised __“that his *name* be not put out of Israel,”__ and the man who refuses is shamed as one who __“will not *build up his brother’s house*”__ (Deuteronomy 25:6, 9) — in the law’s own grammar, building a house and raising a name are one act.
So Boaz declares he has taken Ruth __“to *raise up the name of the dead* upon his inheritance”__ (Ruth 4:10); the elders bless her as one come to __“*build the house*”__ (Ruth 4:11); and the house that wedding built was the house of *David* (Ruth 4:17) — the very house God would answer with a house for His own name.

A bride under the wing, a name raised, a house built — and in the fulness of time, a Son of that house who is Himself the temple.
The symbols do not merely repeat; they compound.

The symbol gathers up the ones before it.
The sym:sym-gospel[gospel] is the covenant _announced_; the sym:sym-way[way], the sym:sym-truth[truth], and the sym:sym-life[life] are the covenant _embodied_; the name is the covenant _owned_ — taken upon yourself as a sym:sym-marriage[bride] takes her husband’s, to keep or to empty.
Most who cry __“Lord, Lord”__ wear it for nothing.
To bear it in truth is to keep the covenant of the One in whom the name dwells — and so to be sym:sym-knowing[known] by Him in that day.
And the name owned is also written — impressed on its bearers like a signet in wax.
Where God sets it, what it says, and what counterfeit stamps the same two places — that is the seal, and it is the link:/books/symbolic-language/the-seal/[Seal] chapter.

The gospel's last command is to *disciple* the nations, and everyone thinks he knows what the word means: a follower, a learner, a student of Jesus.
The dictionary is not wrong; it is empty.
A learner of *what*?
Scripture does not leave the answer open — it defines the word exactly once, and it puts the definition in the mouth of the law itself:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 8:16]
____
Bind up the testimony, *seal the law* among my *disciples*.
____

The Old Testament's word for disciples — _limmudim_, the taught ones — appears here in the law's own custody clause.
A disciple is where the law is kept when the testimony is bound: the scroll sealed in a living person.
Isaiah uses the word once more, as a promise: __“all thy children shall be *taught of the LORD*”__ (Isaiah 54:13) — _limmudei YHWH_, the LORD's own disciples — and Jesus quotes that very line for His hearers (John 6:45).

[discrete]
=== The Gates

Jesus did not describe discipleship as a mood of admiration.
He stated its terms, and three times He said *cannot*:

* __“If any man come to me, and *hate not* his father, and mother… he *cannot* be my disciple”__ (Luke 14:26)
* __“whosoever doth not *bear his cross*, and come after me, *cannot* be my disciple”__ (Luke 14:27)
* __“whosoever he be of you that *forsaketh not all* that he hath, he *cannot* be my disciple”__ (Luke 14:33)

These are gates, not growth curves — and inside the gates He named the marks: __“If ye *continue in my word*, then are ye my disciples *indeed*”__ (John 8:31); __“By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have sym:sym-love[love] one to another”__ (John 13:35) — and love is the keeping of the commandments (1 John 5:3); __“Herein is my Father glorified, that ye bear much sym:sym-fruit[fruit]; so shall ye be my disciples”__ (John 15:8) — and fruit is works.
_Indeed_ is the word to weigh: it is spoken to men who had just *believed* (John 8:30-31) — believed as a profession believes: His word accounted factual and worth trusting, an assent even __“the devils”__ manage, who __“believe, and tremble”__ (James 2:19).
Scripture's full *belief* walks: __“He that *believeth* on the Son hath eternal life; but he that *obeyeth not* the Son shall not see life”__ (John 3:36, ASV) — one verse, and the opposite of believing is disobeying.
So He hands the professors the walking itself as the test: continue in the word, and __“then are ye my disciples indeed.”__

[discrete]
=== Baptized into the Name

The commission binds the entry rite to the definition: __“baptizing them *in the* sym:sym-name[name] of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost”__ (Matthew 28:19).
The sym:sym-name[NAME] is the covenant — and baptism places the disciple *into* it: __“buried with him by baptism… even so we also should *walk* in newness of life”__ (Romans 6:4); __“as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have *put on* Christ”__ (Galatians 3:27) — the covenant worn as a sym:sym-garment[garment].
And the covenant one is baptized into has stated content:

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 31:33]
____
this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel… I will put my *law* in their inward parts, and *write it in their hearts*.
____

The new covenant is not the law's retirement; it is the law's change of address — from tables of stone to the tables of the heart.
Jeremiah's promise and Isaiah's seal are one act described twice: the law, written within.
To be baptized into the Name is to enroll in that covenant — the heart handed in as the next table to be written.

[discrete]
=== As His Master

The church has a word for the goal of discipleship — *Christlikeness* — and the word is correct; it has simply been left undefined.
Jesus defined it:

[quote.scripture, Luke 6:40]
____
The disciple is not above his master: but every one that is *perfect* shall be *as his master*.
____

The disciple's finish line is likeness.
Then everything hangs on one question: what is the Master like?
He is the One of whom the Father said, __“obey his voice… for *my name is in him*”__ (Exodus 23:21); who kept His own in that name (John 17:11); and who set the pattern in a single sentence:

[quote.scripture, John 15:10]
____
If ye *keep my commandments*, ye shall abide in my love; even as *I have kept my Father's commandments*, and abide in his love.
____

He kept the law — perfectly: __“Which of you convinceth me of sin?”__ (John 8:46); not to destroy but to fulfil (Matthew 5:17).
To become like Him is therefore not a sentiment; it has exact content: __“He that saith he abideth in him ought himself also *so to walk, even as he walked*”__ (1 John 2:6).
He walked in the commandments.
Christlikeness *is* the law sealed within — the consensus's own word, given the Master's own content.

[discrete]
=== Whose Works?

Becoming as the master is a warning before it is a promise: Jesus hung the sentence on a question about guides — __“Can the blind lead the blind? shall they not both fall into the ditch?”__ (Luke 6:39).
Israel had other masters, with disciples of their own (Mark 2:18), and He split their authority down the middle:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 23:2-3]
____
The scribes and the Pharisees sit in *Moses' seat*: all therefore whatsoever they *bid you observe*, that observe and do; but do not ye after their *works*: for they say, and do not.
____

What they relay from Moses' seat is commanded — observe and do; their own *works* are refused in the same breath, for a work is a deed executing a command, and their deeds executed their own legislation.
The Hebrew Matthew reads the seeming concession out of the verse — its verb is singular: __“all that *he* says to you, keep and do; but according to their *ordinances* and their deeds, do not do”__ — Moses speaking from the seat, and both columns of the refusal theirs.
__“They say, and do not”__ falls wholly on the men in the seat, and __“their deeds”__ — _ma'aseihem_, their *works* — stand written beside their ordinances as the deeds that execute them.
He read the charge to their face: __“Why do ye also *transgress the commandment of God* by your *tradition*?… in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the *commandments of men*”__ (Matthew 15:3, 9) — and the Hebrew again writes the legal terms into the verse: your _taqqanot_, your *enactments*, and _mitzvat anashim_, a *commandment of men* learned by rote.
The same scene ends in the ditch: __“they be *blind leaders of the blind*. And if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch”__ (Matthew 15:14) — masters whose disciples, perfected, are as they are.

The prophets had already given this fork its legal name.
Micah's indictment of Israel names the crime as keeping — the covenant's own verb — sworn to the wrong legislator:

[quote.scripture, Micah 6:16]
____
For the *statutes of Omri* are *kept*, and all the *works of the house of Ahab*, and ye walk in their counsels; that I should make thee a desolation…
____

__“Kept”__ is _shamar_, the verb of keeping the commandments, here spent on a king's statutes; evil works are another legislator's statutes kept.
Jehoshaphat is the bright mirror: he __“walked in his *commandments*, and not after the *doings* of Israel”__ (2 Chronicles 17:4) — one nation, two legislators, and every deed executing one or the other.

Moses legislated the audit in advance: the prophet whose sign comes to pass, but who teaches departure from the commandments, is refused — __“ye shall walk after the LORD your God, and fear him, and *keep his commandments*”__ (Deuteronomy 13:4).
The judgment scene runs on that statute: the pleaders of __“many *powers*”__ claim, in the Greek, _dynameis_, and in the Hebrew Gospel _otot_, *signs* — no works are pleaded, and works are the verdict: __“depart from me, ye that *work lawlessness*”__ (Matthew 7:22-23), which is Psalm 6:8 word for word: __“depart from me, all ye *workers of iniquity*.”__
Signs prove power; works prove whose command — and whose command, whose disciple.

[discrete]
=== The Name on the Forehead

The road that begins in baptism ends where the next chapter, link:/books/symbolic-language/the-seal/[The Seal], ends: __“a Lamb stood on the mount Sion, and with him an hundred forty and four thousand, having *his Father's name written in their foreheads*”__ (Revelation 14:1); __“I will *write upon him the name* of my God”__ (Revelation 3:12).
Baptized into the Name; perfected as the Master in whom the Name is; sealed with the Name at the last — the disciple's whole arc is one Name carried from water to forehead, and the Name carries the law.
Seal the law among my disciples: the commission, Isaiah's clause, and the 144,000 are one sentence spoken three times.
