    ref: "Matthew 13:45-46"
---
The kingdom of heaven is likened to a *merchant man* seeking *goodly pearls*, who finds *one pearl of great price*, sells all that he has, and buys it.
Jesus left this parable unkeyed — no interpretation is recorded — so the derivation stands where the link:/books/symbolic-language/the-parables-of-the-kingdom/[Parables of the Kingdom] chapter left it: on *our* method alone, tested like everything else and held fast if it proves good.

The method begins with the parable's own key words: a *merchant*; *goodly* — simply *good*; and *one* sym:sym-pearl[pearl] — for *one* is no mere count.
Of all the goodly pearls the merchant finds, he sells everything for exactly one, and one signals what it signals everywhere in Scripture: *complete*, *whole*, undivided — a thing nothing can be added to.
Search those words through Scripture, and they gather at one address.

[discrete]
=== Three Words, Three Places

The *pearls* come first, and the King James buried them.
The link:/books/symbolic-language/the-parables-of-the-kingdom/[Parables of the Kingdom] chapter already dug them out from under the King James’ __“rubies”__: the Hebrew _peninim_ is, by Strong's own definition, __“probably *a pearl* (as round).”__
Recovered, the pearls keep exactly the parable's company: sym:sym-wisdom[Wisdom] is priced above *pearls* (Proverbs 3:15; 8:11; Job 28:18) — and the seeker who searches for her __“as for *hid treasures*”__ (Proverbs 2:4) is himself the merchant of the parable.
And the virtuous woman — the one sym:sym-marriage[bride] — is __“far above *pearls*”__ (Proverbs 31:10), drawn up out of the sym:sym-sea[sea] of the nations.

Now the *merchant* and his *good*.
Solomon prices wisdom in the merchant's own terms — __“For the *merchandise* of it is better than the merchandise of silver”__ (Proverbs 3:14) — and Scripture stamps that merchandise *good* in exactly two more places in all its pages.
The first is the woman of this same book — __“her *merchandise* is *good*”__ (Proverbs 31:18) — and in the Hebrew this is no echo but a *quotation*: letter for letter the clause of 3:14, כִּי־טוֹב סַחְרָהּ, __“for her merchandise is good.”__
The second is the parable itself: the kingdom's __“*merchant* man, seeking *goodly* pearls”__ (Matthew 13:45).
Three texts, one thread — sym:sym-wisdom[wisdom], the woman, the sym:sym-pearl[pearl]: the *good merchandise*.

Proverbs interchanges the subject in its own grammar: the find-verb of 3:13 returns exactly twice in the book — __“whoso findeth *me*”__ (8:35, Wisdom speaking) and __“whoso findeth *a wife*”__ (18:22).
Wisdom and the bride hold one slot in Solomon's sentences, and the parable's pearl prices them both.
The merchant's vocabulary has led to two poems — wisdom's and the bride's — and this book reads poems like these on the bare letters.

[discrete]
=== The Poems Rendered Whole

What follows is each poem rendered afresh from the bare letters.
Where the plain King James reading is best, it stands untouched; every word changed is changed to an attested sense of the same letters, and every change is weighed, word by word, before this chapter ends.
Nothing here unseats the wife and mother of the plain reading — both readings run at once.
First, hear the poems clean.

[quote.scripture, Proverbs 3:13-20 — rendered from the letters]
____
Blessed is the man that findeth sym:sym-wisdom[wisdom], and the man that *draweth out* sym:sym-understanding[understanding].
For the gain of her *going-round* is better than the *going-round* of silver, and her *harvest* than fine gold.
She is more *bright* than sym:sym-pearl[pearls]: and all thy delights are not to be compared unto her.
*Length and appropriateness of days* is in her *right hand*; and in her left hand riches and *shining*.
Her ways are ways of *splendour*, and all her paths are *wholeness*.
She is a sym:sym-tree[tree] of life to them that lay hold upon her: and blessed is every one that *holdeth her fast*.
The LORD by wisdom hath founded the earth; by understanding hath he *established* the heavens.
By his knowledge the depths were *broken open*, and the *skies* drop down the dew.
____

[quote.scripture, Proverbs 31:10-31 — rendered from the letters]
____
A woman of valour who can find? for her price is far above sym:sym-pearl[pearls].
The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her, and gain shall *never diminish*.
She doeth him good and not evil all the days of her life.
She seeketh wool, and flax, and worketh willingly with her *palms*.
She is like the ships of *the one who travels round*; she bringeth her sym:sym-bread[bread] *from afar*.
She riseth also while it is yet sym:sym-night[night], and giveth *the covenant's* sym:sym-meat[meat] to her household, and *the appointed portion* to her maidens.
She considereth a sym:sym-field[field], and *taketh* it: with the sym:sym-fruit[fruit] of her *palms* she planteth a vineyard.
She girdeth her loins with *strength*, and strengtheneth her arms.
She *tasteth that it is good*, her merchandise: her sym:sym-lamp[lamp] goeth not out *in the night*.
She layeth her hands to the spindle, and her *palms hold fast* *the circuit*.
She spreadeth out her *palm* to the sym:sym-poor[poor]; yea, she reacheth forth her hands to the sym:sym-poor[needy].
She is not *worried by the whiteness* for her household: for all her household are clothed *in double*.
She maketh herself coverings; her clothing is *white linen* and purple.
Her husband is known in the sym:sym-door[gates], when he sitteth among the sym:sym-elders[*elders*] of the land.
She maketh *linen wraps*, and selleth them; and delivereth girdles unto the *merchant*.
Strength and *splendour* are her clothing; and she *laugheth at the last day*.
She openeth her mouth with sym:sym-wisdom[wisdom]; and in her tongue is the law of kindness.
She *keepeth the watch* over the *walkings* of her household, and eateth not the sym:sym-bread[bread] of *idleness*.
Her sons arise, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he *maketh her shine*.
Many daughters have done valiantly, but thou hast *gone up above them all*.
Charm is a lie, and beauty a *vapour*: a woman that feareth the LORD, *she it is that shall shine*.
Give her of the fruit of her hands; and let her own works *make her shine in the* sym:sym-door[gates].
____

[discrete]
=== The Poems in Plain Language

The link:/books/symbolic-language/sun-moon-and-stars/[Sun, Moon, and Stars] chapter read the lights: the sym:sym-sun[sun] the Father and the husband; the sym:sym-moon[moon] the sym:sym-faithful-witness[faithful witness] — the Son toward His Father, the sym:sym-marriage[bride] toward her Bridegroom; the sym:sym-stars[stars] the righteous, gathered into the twelve; the sym:sym-elders[elders] seated among the host; and the gates of the sky's tabernacle, through which the lights come and go.
Lay the poems against that sky, line by line, and every line finds its station.

__“She riseth also while it is yet night… her lamp goeth not out in the night”__ (31:15, 18).
Of all the lights a reader has ever seen, exactly one rises as the dark falls and burns until morning: the *full moon*, which climbs the east gate at sunset and holds the sky the whole night through.
And what she serves her household is the calendar's own food — __“the covenant's meat… the appointed portion”__: the portion-word is _choq_, the __“ordinances of the sym:sym-moon[moon] and of the sym:sym-stars[stars]”__ by sym:sym-night[night] (Jeremiah 31:35).

__“She is more bright than pearls”__ (3:15).
__“Bright”__ is the King James’ own word for the moon — __“the *moon* walking in *brightness*”__ (Job 31:26) — the comparison priced in the moon-verse's own vocabulary.

__“Length and appropriateness of days is in her right hand; and in her left hand riches and shining”__ (3:16).
The month's own length — twenty-nine days or thirty — is declared at her fulness, and declared *fitting*: the appointed day, the day of meeting, sym:sym-meat[meat] given __“in *due season*”__ (Matthew 24:45).
And Strong's reads the right-hand word as __“locally, the south,”__ and the left-hand word as __“properly dark (as enveloped)”__ — the north: days in her bright hand, shining even in her dark one.

__“She worketh willingly with her palms… her palms hold fast the circuit… She spreadeth out her palm to the poor”__ (31:13, 19, 20).
The poem says *palm* — _kaph_ — where it could have said hand, and keeps the two words distinct inside single verses.
And _kaph_ is a shape before it is a limb: Strong's spends the word on every *curved, hollow container* — the palm, the sole, the pans of the tabernacle, the bowl of a spoon — a rounded vessel made to *hold* and to *cover*.
It is the palm God laid over Moses while the glory passed by (Exodus 33:22); and here it is the curved cup that receives the Bridegroom's light and *holds fast the circuit*, carrying it round the year — then opens toward the sym:sym-poor[poor], the King's own signature: __“He shall deliver the needy when he crieth; the *poor* also”__ (Psalm 72:12), in the very psalm where they fear Him __“with the sun and *before the face of* the moon”__ through all revolutions of time (72:5, as the letters run).

__“She considereth a field, and taketh it: with the fruit of her palms she planteth a vineyard. She girdeth her loins with strength”__ (31:16-17).
This is the Bridegroom's own record in parable: He *planted the vineyard* (Matthew 21:33) — and Isaiah names it, __“the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of *Israel*”__ (Isaiah 5:7) — and He *bought the field* for the treasure hidden in it, and __“the field is the *world*”__ (Matthew 13:44, 38).
And she *strengthens* what she plants, where the counterfeit of the last chapter's plan __“didst *weaken* the nations”__ (Isaiah 14:12) and wears out the saints (Daniel 7:25): one plants and strengthens, the other wears down.

__“She tasteth that it is good, her merchandise”__ (31:18).
The words first spoken over light itself — __“and God saw the light, that it was *good*”__ (Genesis 1:4) — tasted now over the *good merchandise* of the three texts.

__“She is not worried by the whiteness for her household: for all her household are clothed in double… her clothing is white linen and purple”__ (31:21-22).
Her household are the sym:sym-stars[stars], and they want for no light: they are clothed *in double* — the reading the oldest translations kept — and her own weave is _shesh_, *white linen* by definition.

__“Her husband is known in the gates, when he sitteth among the elders of the land”__ (31:23) — __“and let her own works make her shine in the gates”__ (31:31).
Her husband, the sun of this portrait, is *known in the gates* — the doors of his own circuit through the twelve — and he sits among the sym:sym-elders[*elders*], the bench the Sun, Moon, and Stars chapter seated among the host of heaven.
Her works shine at the same doors: the gates her fulness passes through, each one, the city says, a single pearl.

__“Her sons arise, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he maketh her shine”__ (31:28).
The verb is _halal_, whose first sense is *to shine*: he makes her shine, as the sun makes the moon.

__“Strength and splendour are her clothing; and she laugheth at the last day”__ (31:25).
Beneath the laugh, in the same letters, stands the _shachaq_ — the sky where the sym:sym-faithful-witness[faithful witness] is established (Psalm 89:37) — and she can laugh at the day because she knows its date: sym:sym-wisdom[Wisdom] laughs at calamity (Proverbs 1:26) for the reason the psalm gives, __“he seeth that his *day is coming*”__ (Psalm 37:13).

__“She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness”__ (31:26).
That is the nightly speech of the nineteenth Psalm — __“no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard”__: the witness declares, and what she declares is torah, kindly.

Through all of it the poem never says *moon*; the Hebrew of the portrait contains no moon-word at all.
It paints a light that rises in the dark, shines the whole night with a shining her husband gives her, deals the appointed portions, holds the circuit — and withholds the name to the last line.
The Song of Songs supplies what the portrait withheld, singing the same two praise-verbs over the same one-above-the-daughters woman:

[quote.scripture, Song of Solomon 6:9-10]
____
My dove, my undefiled is but *one*; she is the *only one* of her mother, she is the choice one of her that bare her.
The daughters saw her, and *blessed* her; yea, the queens and the concubines, and they *praised* her.
Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, *fair as the* sym:sym-moon[moon], clear as the sym:sym-sun[sun], and terrible as an army with banners?
____

The poem paints the portrait; the Song signs it.

Wisdom's poem reads the same way, line by line.
__“She is a tree of life to them that lay hold upon her: and blessed is every one that holdeth her fast”__ (3:18) — the holding-verb is _tamak_, the verb of the palms holding the circuit, and the verb of Moses’ hands on the mountain, held up *steady* — _emunah_, the faithful-witness word — __“until the going down of the sun,”__ while Joshua *weakened* Amalek — _chalash_, the rare verb of Isaiah 14:12, three occurrences in all of Scripture (Exodus 17:12-13).

__“The LORD by wisdom hath founded the earth; by understanding hath he established the heavens”__ (3:19) — __“established”__ is _konen_, the verb of __“the moon and the stars, which thou hast *ordained*”__ (Psalm 8:3); the wisdom priced above sym:sym-pearl[pearls] is the wisdom that built the sky — __“when he prepared the heavens, *I was there*”__ (Proverbs 8:27).
__“By his knowledge the depths were broken open, and the skies drop down the dew”__ (3:20) — the *broken-open* deeps are Genesis 7:11's, the flood's calendar-stamped ledger; and the __“skies”__ are the _shachaqim_, the witness's own sky, dropping down the dew.

[discrete]
=== The One Pearl of the Night Sky
Mark the pearl's properties as Scripture handles the figure.
It is *one*: the merchant found __“one pearl of great price”__ and stopped collecting, for the kingdom is not a collection but one bride, bought whole.
It is *round and complete*: the roundness sits inside Strong's definition itself.
It is *white* — a bearer of soft, borrowed light out of darkness — and it is born of the *waters*.
Then Revelation prices the city's entrances in it:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 21:21]
____
And the twelve sym:sym-door[gates] were twelve *pearls*; *every several gate was of one pearl*…
____

The Greek doubles the point — _each one_ of the gates, _of one_ pearl — and the Hebrew Revelation doubles it the same way: every *single* gate, of *one* pearl.
Not gates studded with pearls: each gate *is* one pearl — one, complete, whole.
So the pearl, wherever Scripture spends it, is the one complete thing of great price — and it is a *gate*.
Now ask the merchant's question: has the King hung such a thing anywhere in plain sight — one, round, white, complete, and standing at a door?

Look up.
Of all the moon's phases and all the lights of heaven, exactly one is white, round, and complete: the night sky owns precisely one pearl.
And Scripture had already assigned that light its office: the moon appointed for the _moedim_, the appointed times, from the fourth day (Psalm 104:19; Genesis 1:14).

The pairing was set at the pattern's founding: Joseph's dream read the moon as the *mother* (Genesis 37:9-10), and the sun comes out of his chamber __“as a *bridegroom*”__ (Psalm 19:5) — a bridegroom's answering light is his bride, the counterpart the link:/books/symbolic-language/sun-moon-and-stars/[Sun, Moon, and Stars] chapter already seated facing him, moon toward her Bridegroom as the Son is moon toward His Father.

[discrete]
=== The Letters Confirm It

If the pearl has led truly, the letters should be waiting at the same spot — and they are.
Scripture keeps a __“fulness”__ overhead, and the King James buried it exactly as it buried the pearls.
The Hebrew is _keseh_ — Strong's: __“properly, *fulness* or the *full moon*”__ — and most translations render it as what it is:

[quote.scripture, Psalm 81:3, NKJV]
____
Blow the trumpet at the time of the New Moon, at the *full* sym:sym-moon[moon], on our solemn feast day.
____

Here the King James stands nearly alone with its __“in the time appointed”__; the NKJV, the ESV, the NASB, the Jewish Publication Society's version — __“at the full moon for our feast-day”__ — and Smith's Literal Translation all read *full moon*.
And the oldest translation of all leans the same way: the Septuagint, made centuries before Messiah, renders the day __“in the *glorious* day of your feast”__ — the Greek is _eusēmos_, *well-marked, conspicuous*, built on _sēma_, a *sign*, the very root the Greek of Genesis 1:14 hangs the lights on, __“for *signs*.”__
Whatever else those translators heard in _keseh_, they heard the day the sky cannot hide — and of the moon's phases exactly one is conspicuous, while the dark conjunction is the one day the sky shows no sign at all.

The verse does not say __“and”__ between the new moon and the full moon — one day, not two.
Some translations insert an __“and”__ to split them apart; the Hebrew, rendered literally, in its own order, runs the other way — _you shall blow with the new-moon trumpet in the full moon for the day of our festival sacrifice_ — the full moon *is* the head of the month, the feast-day of Numbers 10:10 and 28:11.

Solomon uses the same word for the day the traveling husband returns: __“he will come home at the *full moon*”__ (Proverbs 7:20) — _keseh_ again — and there it is spelled כסא, letter for letter the spelling of _kisse’_, __“throne.”__
The last chapter stood on that identity from the enemy's side; here is the LORD's side of it. Both words grow from one root, _kasah_, to cover, to fill — the throne is the covered seat, the full moon the filled light — and Job holds the two senses up in a single verse: __“He holdeth back the face of *his throne*, and spreadeth *his cloud* upon it”__ (Job 26:9), the veiled face of His full sym:sym-moon[moon].

If it is asked which way the covering runs — whether the throne-word is covered in darkness or covered in light — Scripture describes the throne itself.
Daniel saw the throne-room itself, and every detail belongs to this chapter:

[quote.scripture, Daniel 7:9 — rendered from the Aramaic]
____
I beheld till the *thrones* were *set in place*, and the *Ancient of days* did sit, whose garment was *white as snow*, and the hair of his head like the *pure wool*: his throne was like the *fiery flame*, and his wheels as burning fire.
____

The thrones are *set* — placed like lights in their stations.footnote:dan79set[The King James prints __“the thrones were cast down”__; the Aramaic verb is one of placing, and the newer translations read it so — the thrones were set, not overthrown.]
And the title under __“Ancient of days”__ is built on a root of moving onward, going before — read once, He is the Ancient of Days; read again, He is the *Foremost of Days*: the One at the head of the days, seated where the days begin.
His garment white as snow, His hair like the pure wool, His throne flame, His wheels burning fire — and the plural on __“wheels”__ is the ending this book met on Daniel's sevens: an intensive, not a count — *the wheel complete*, the perfect circle of fire.

Whiteness enthroned on light; brightness round about it, __“as the appearance of the sym:sym-bow[bow] that is in the sym:sym-cloud[cloud] in the day of rain”__ (Ezekiel 1:26-28); and its Occupant __“coverest thyself with *light* as with a garment”__ (Psalm 104:2).
If the throne is the _keseh_, Daniel's vision draws what the letters spell: the full moons set in their stations, and the Head of Days taking His seat — white, complete, covered in light — where the month begins.

The psalm that gave this book the sym:sym-faithful-witness[faithful witness] link:/books/symbolic-language/sun-moon-and-stars/[already sets the throne] as the sym:sym-sun[sun] and as the sym:sym-moon[moon] — Psalm 89:36-37 — plain simile, not wordplay, and the throne is a throne of light.footnote:fn26thronepsalm[Derived in the link:/books/symbolic-language/sun-moon-and-stars/[Sun, Moon, and Stars] chapter.]
Where darkness stands near it, it stands *outside*, as a veil: __“clouds and darkness are *round about* him”__ (Psalm 97:2) — round about, not within — the cloud of Job 26:9 spread *upon* the face, holding the light back.
The _keseh_ is covered in light; only the counterfeit is covered in dark.

[discrete]
=== The Gate That Opens

The sky is built like a sanctuary — the tabernacle Psalm 19 pitched for the sun — and its front, like the tabernacle's, faces the sunrise, the sym:sym-east[east].
Now hear Ezekiel on the gates of the house:

[quote.scripture, Ezekiel 46:1]
____
Thus saith the Lord GOD; The sym:sym-door[gate] of the inner court that looketh toward the sym:sym-east[east] shall be *shut the six working days*; but on the *sabbath* it shall be opened, and in the day of the *new* sym:sym-moon[moon] it shall be opened.
____

Three kinds of days — working days, sabbaths, new-moon days (Amos knew the third kind too: __“When will the *new moon* be gone, that we may sell corn?”__ Amos 8:5) — and on the day that begins the month, the east gate stands open.
A gate is opened because something is meant to come through it.
And exactly one phase enters by the east gate at the fall of night: the *full* moon enters in the east at the hour the portrait already fixed — through the front door of the sky's tabernacle, the faithful witness at maximum.

The sliver, by contrast, is hunted low in the *west*, at sunset, beside the sun — and the sheepfold has a rule about entrances:

[quote.scripture, John 10:1-2]
____
Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that entereth not by the sym:sym-door[door] into the sheepfold, but *climbeth up some other way*, the same is a *thief* and a robber.
But he that entereth in by the sym:sym-door[door] is the *shepherd* of the sheep.
____

The prince of Ezekiel's house comes and goes __“by the way of the gate that looketh toward the *east*”__ (Ezekiel 46:12).
The true light enters at the front sym:sym-door[gate]; the counterfeit climbs in from the dark side — which is precisely the address his heart chose in the last chapter.

[discrete]
=== One Pearl, One Gate

Now set the pieces together.
The pearl is the full moon; the city's pearl-gates are His appointed times — for the _moedim_ are, as the last chapter read the word, *meetings*: the fixed days on which the King receives.
Twelve gates; twelve months of full moons; the sym:sym-stars[stars] of God gathered into the twelve constellations, the __“Mazzaroth”__ brought forth __“in his season”__ (Job 38:32), through which the full moon makes its yearly round.
And there Solomon's woman collects what her portrait promised — praised in the gates her fulness passes through, her husband at home among the elders.

The merchant who sold all he had for *one pearl of great price* was not buying jewelry.
He was buying his entry at the King's gate — the appointed time of meeting — and Isaiah had already welded the paired parables into one sentence: __“sym:sym-wisdom[wisdom] and knowledge shall be the stability of thy *times*… the sym:sym-fear[fear] of the LORD is his *treasure*”__ (Isaiah 33:6).
The treasure and the times; the pearl and the gate.

__“It is the glory of God to *conceal* a thing: but the honour of kings is to *search out* a matter”__ (Proverbs 25:2) — He hid the pearl where only a merchant who would sell everything looks.

[discrete]
=== Pearls Before Swine

Jesus spent the pearl-word one other time, and it is a warning:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 7:6]
____
Give not that which is *holy* unto the sym:sym-dog[dogs], neither cast ye your *pearls* before *swine*, lest they *trample them under their feet*, and turn again and rend you.
____

The dogs and the swine are one family — unclean sym:sym-beast[beasts], the nations outside the covenant table.
And what swine do to pearls is exactly what Scripture says the nations do to holy things: they tread them underfoot — __“it is given unto the *Gentiles*: and the holy city shall they *tread under foot*”__ (Revelation 11:2); the sanctuary and the host __“*trodden under foot*”__ (Daniel 8:13); __“Jerusalem shall be *trodden down* of the Gentiles, until the *times* of the Gentiles be fulfilled”__ (Luke 21:24).

Mark the last word of that sentence: what the trampling runs until is a matter of *times*.
If the pearl is the appointed time of meeting, the warning reads whole: hand the holy times to the nations and they will not keep them — they will trample them, and turn and rend the hand that gave them.
Daniel named the plan — to change the times and the laws; this verse is the Lord's advance notice of how the theft would look on the ground — the pearl underfoot.

[discrete]
=== The Two Moons

Read this chapter and the last as the pair they are.
The enemy raises the moon covered in *darkness*; the LORD's sign is the same seat covered in *light* — the Father's whole face borne through the dark.
One moon reflects everything; the other reflects nothing, for its source produces only dark.
One enters by the door; the other climbs up some other way.

The sky itself stages the ambition, for the two moons stand in two different places: the full moon, standing always opposite, can never come between; only the moon covered in darkness can stand *over* the sun — slide before his face and put out the day at noon — and blot the sym:sym-stars[stars] from the same sky.
That is the plan of the last chapter drawn in one picture — __“Woe unto them… that put *darkness for light*, and *light for darkness*”__ (Isaiah 5:20).

The sym:sym-stars[stars] — the righteous, who keep time — follow one moon or the other.
That is why the parable's merchant sells *all*: the pearl is not an ornament on the kingdom; it is the gate into it, and there has only ever been one seller who could ask that price and one buyer who paid it gladly.

Grade this chapter the way the Parables of the Kingdom chapter graded everything, for the method matters more than any single finding.
Every link stands in the text: the pearl-word under the King James’ __“rubies”__; the city's gates each of *one pearl*; the moon set over the _moedim_ from the fourth day; the fulness-word under __“throne”__ and __“time appointed”__ confirming where the pearl had already led; the east gate opened on the new-moon day; and the two poems rendered whole on the bare letters, every departure weighed word by word.
The chain that joins the links is a reading — this book's reading, offered to be tested, not swallowed.

The reckoning that follows from it — where the month truly begins, how the sabbaths fall, what history did to the calendar and what the sky and the records of the nations still testify — is a book of its own.footnote:fn26ttt[The complete case is made in _Time Tested Tradition: The Renewed Biblical Calendar_.]
This chapter needs only the symbol.
The kingdom has a gate; the gate is one complete pearl; and the merchant who understands what is being sold does not haggle.

[discrete]
=== Every Word Weighed

The rule of the link:/books/symbolic-language/what-is-the-point/[What Is the Point?] chapter cuts both ways: the pointing gets a vote, not a veto — and neither does the re-reading, until the letters and the witnesses agree.
Here, then, is every departure, weighed; whatever is not listed is the King James untouched.

*In wisdom's poem (Proverbs 3:13-20):*

- __draweth out__ (3:13) — _puq_, Strong's “to issue, draw out”; the King James’ “getteth” flattens a verb of drawing forth.
- __going-round__ (3:14) — _sachar_, “to travel round (as a pedlar); traffic” — the merchant-word of 31:14, 18; rendered by its own root-sense.
- __harvest__ (3:14) — _tevuah_, “income, i.e. produce”; the King James renders it “increase” and “fruits” elsewhere — the field-word, kept agricultural.
- __bright__ (3:15) — _yaqar_: the King James’ own rendering at Job 31:26 — “the moon walking in *brightness*” — the one place it describes a light.
- __pearls__ (3:15; 31:10) — _peninim_, Strong's “probably a pearl (as round)”; the chapter's founding recovery.
- __length and appropriateness of days / shining__ (3:16) — the root under _orek_ keeps a second sense in the same letters: _arik_, __“it was not *meet* for us”__ (Ezra 4:14), Strong's __“reaching to a given point; to suit”__ — the days counted *and* fitted; and _kavod_ is glory as Scripture displays it, radiance — __“Arise, *shine*; for thy light is come, and the *glory* of the LORD is risen upon thee”__ (Isaiah 60:1).
- __splendour / wholeness__ (3:17) — _noam_, “agreeableness, i.e. delight, suitableness, splendor”; _shalom_, “safe, i.e. well, happy... completeness” — peace as the whole and unbroken.
- __holdeth her fast__ (3:18) — _tamak_, “to sustain; to obtain, keep fast” — the verb of 31:19.
- __established__ (3:19) — _konen_ (H3559), the verb of Psalm 8:3, “the moon and the stars, which thou hast *ordained*.”
- __broken open / skies__ (3:20) — _baqa_, the verb of Genesis 7:11 (“were all the fountains of the great deep *broken up*”); _shachaqim_, the sky-word of Psalm 89:37.

*In the bride's portrait (Proverbs 31:10-31):*

- __never diminish__ (31:11) — _chaser_: Strong's King James column reads “decrease, abated, fail” — the gain that does not wane.
- __palms__ (31:13, 16, 19, 20) — _kaph_, “the hollow hand or palm,” kept visible because the poem itself sets _kaph_ beside _yad_ inside single verses (vv19-20): the palm and the hand are distinguished by the poet, not by us.
- __the one who travels round__ (31:14) — _sachar_ again, the same going-round as 3:14.
- __taketh it__ (31:16) — the written verb is _laqach_, to *take*; the King James prints __“buyeth it.”__
- __the covenant's meat / the appointed portion__ (31:15) — _teref_ is the noun of Psalm 111:5, “he hath given *meat* unto them that fear him: he will ever be mindful of his *covenant*”; _choq_ is “an enactment; an appointment (of time)” — the King James’ own “set time” (Job 14:13), and the word of Jeremiah 31:35's moon-and-stars ordinances.
- __tasteth that it is good / in the night__ (31:18) — the Hebrew order restored: טָעֲמָה כִּי־טוֹב — “she tasteth that *it is good*,” the _ki tov_ spoken over the light (Genesis 1:4); “in the night” is the written text (the kethib).
- __the circuit__ (31:19) — _pelekh_, “from an unused root meaning to be round; a circuit... also a spindle (as whirled)”; the King James itself renders it as a district (“part,” Nehemiah 3). Both spin: the housewife's whorl and the sky's round.
- __not worried by the whiteness / in double__ (31:21) — _yare_ is fear in the sense of anxious care, and _sheleg_, snow, is Scripture's standard of *whiteness* (__“white as snow,”__ Isaiah 1:18); and the letters שנים read as _shnayim_, “double”: so the Septuagint (“garments of double texture”), the Vulgate, and Smith's Literal Translation; the pointing reads _shanim_, “scarlet.” The elder witnesses carry the double; the same letters also spell “years” — a revolution of time.
- __white linen__ (31:22) — _shesh_, “bleached stuff, i.e. white linen” — the whiteness sits inside the plain word; the King James’ “silk” is the departure, not ours.
- __laugheth at the last day__ (31:25) — _sachaq_ + _le-yom acharon_: so Young's Literal (“she rejoiceth at a latter day”), the Douay-Rheims (“she shall laugh in the latter day”), and Smith's Literal; the identical phrase is “the *last day*” at Isaiah 30:8. And unpointed, שחק is also _shachaq_ — the witness's sky — a second reading standing in the letters.
- __keepeth the watch / walkings__ (31:27) — _tsofiyah_, the watchman's verb (“I have made thee a *watchman*,” Ezekiel 3:17); _halichot_, “a walking, a procession” — the family of Job 31:26's moon “*walking* in brightness.”
- __maketh her shine / she it is that shall shine / make her shine in the gates__ (31:28, 30, 31) — _halal_, whose base sense is “to *shine*” before it is “to praise” (the King James’ own “when his candle *shined*,” Job 29:3; “the moon walking in brightness” verse sits in the same field): to praise her is to make her shine, and both senses are true at once.
- __gone up above them all__ (31:29) — _alah_, “thou hast gone up”: so Young's and Smith's, literally.
- __vapour__ (31:30) — _hevel_, “breath, vapour” — Ecclesiastes’ word, rendered literally.

Weigh them all; the reading asks no favors.
Every changed word is an attested sense of the very letters the scribes counted, most of them the King James’ own renderings from other verses — and the elder witnesses, the Greek and the Latin, already read the doubled garments a thousand years before the points were fixed.
The pointing keeps the housewife; the letters keep the housewife *and* the light she was always painted from.
Both are true — that is how this language testifies.

The appointed times the pearl governs are counted in sevens — and the word Scripture counts them with is the next chapter.

description: "The Exodus is not only history; it is the similitude of the end. The plagues replay in the vials, the call 'Come out of her, my people' repeats 'let my people go,' the pursuer sinks like a stone in both stories, and the victors stand on a sea of glass singing the song of Moses and the Lamb. The verdict is not the going down — everyone goes into the waters — but the not rising: Babylon sinks and 'shall not rise'; Jonah, the Messiah, and the baptized come up."
og_title: "The Fall of Babylon — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "Thus shall Babylon sink, and shall not rise from the evil that I will bring upon her."
    ref: "Jeremiah 51:64"
---
When the victors over the sym:sym-beast[beast] stand on the sea of glass at the end of the story, listen to what they sing:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 15:2-3]
____
And I saw as it were a sym:sym-sea[sea] *of glass* mingled with fire: and them that had gotten the *victory over the* sym:sym-beast[beast]… And they sing the *song of Moses* the servant of God, and the *song of the* sym:sym-lamb[Lamb]…
____

Why the song of _Moses_ — the song Israel sang on the far shore of the Red sea (Exodus 15:1)?
Because the deliverance they have just come through is the same deliverance.
The Exodus is not only history; it is the similitude of the Fall of Babylon — scene for scene, as Jonah was scene for scene the Passion.
Lay the two side by side.

[discrete]
=== The Plagues Replayed

The first plague turned the waters of Egypt to blood; the vials turn the sym:sym-sea[sea] and rivers to blood, and this time link:/books/symbolic-language/sea-and-waters/[the interpretation is spoken aloud] (Revelation 16:6).footnote:fn28bloodtodrink[The vial verses are quoted and worked in full in the link:/books/symbolic-language/sea-and-waters/[Sea & Waters] chapter.]
The waters are __“peoples, and multitudes, and nations”__ (Revelation 17:15) — the equation the sign-of-Jonah chapter first put to work — so waters turned to blood are death upon the peoples, their own shed blood given back to them; the Sea study in Part Six works the full equation.

The hands that wield the plagues are the same office.
Look at the commission of the two witnesses:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 11:6]
____
These have power to shut heaven, that it rain not in the days of their prophecy: and have power over waters to *turn them to blood*, and to *smite the earth with all plagues*, as often as they will.
____

These are Moses and Aaron’s credentials, reissued at the end of the age.
Pharaoh had his court magicians; Babylon has her sorceries (Revelation 18:23).
The contest is the same contest, at full scale.

[discrete]
=== The Rod, the Serpent, and the Rod Again

The contest opened, both times, with one enacted sign — a similitude acted out before a word was argued.
__“What is that in thine hand? And he said, A rod. And he said, Cast it on the ground. And he cast it on the ground, and it became a *serpent*”__ (Exodus 4:2-3).
The rod is no neutral stick: the Hebrew _matteh_ means *staff* and *tribe* in one word — when the princes bring twelve rods, they are the twelve tribes by the language itself (Numbers 17:2) — and Aaron's rod is the rod __“for the house of *Levi*”__ (Numbers 17:8): the priesthood in his hand.
Cast to the earth, the priesthood-rod turns serpent — and before Pharaoh the word sharpens: there it becomes a _tannin_, a sym:sym-dragon[dragon], the devouring kingdom — and __“Aaron's rod *swallowed up* their rods”__ (Exodus 7:12).
The priesthood, gone serpentine, does not merely join the dragons of the nations; it *swallows* them and rides what remains.
John saw where that ends:

[quote.scripture, "Revelation 17:5, 9, 18"]
____
And upon her *forehead* was a name written, MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE *MOTHER OF HARLOTS*… The seven heads are seven sym:sym-mountain[mountains], on which the *woman sitteth*… And the woman which thou sawest is that *great city*, which *reigneth over the kings of the earth*.
____

Mark who can wear that name.
A sym:sym-harlot[harlot] is not an outsider; she is a wife gone traitor — harlotry is covenant *defected*, and only a covenant people can commit it: __“How is the *faithful city* become an harlot!”__ (Isaiah 1:21).
And this great city is identified by its crime scene: __“the great city, which spiritually is called Sodom and sym:sym-egypt[Egypt], *where also our Lord was crucified*”__ (Revelation 11:8) — Jerusalem.
The woman riding the sym:sym-beast[beast] is the covenant order gone serpent — Aaron's rod cast down, astride the seven heads it swallowed — the *mother* whose daughter-harlots learned the trade in her house.
And she wears her name where the sym:sym-seal[seal] goes: upon the forehead — the counterfeit inscription in the counterfeit place.

Jeremiah's oracle even fixes where the last Babylon sits.
__“Your *mother* shall be sore confounded… behold, the *hindermost of the nations* shall be a wilderness”__ (Jeremiah 50:12).
Scripture's compass faces sym:sym-east[east] — _qedem_ is at once “east” and “front” — so the hindermost of the nations is the *westernmost*: the same word names the __“hinder sea,”__ the western sea (Deuteronomy 11:24; Zechariah 14:8).
The last Babylon sits at the far west of the nations: a bloc of seven sym:sym-mountain[mountains] that even counts itself as seven, ridden by the city that killed the prophets, its base of power the westernmost nation of them all.

The similitude has a third act, and it was in Moses' hand from the beginning.
__“Put forth thine hand, and take it by the *tail*. And he put forth his hand, and caught it, and it became a *rod* in his hand”__ (Exodus 4:4).
Every word is loaded.
The tail is decoded in-text by Isaiah: __“the prophet that teacheth lies, he is the *tail*”__ (Isaiah 9:15) — the serpent is seized at its lying-prophet end.
And watch the dragon wield that member:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 12:4]
____
And his *tail* drew the third part of the sym:sym-stars[stars] of heaven, and did cast them to the earth.
____

The stars are the saints, and Daniel shows the same fall with the trampling included: the horn __“cast down some of the host and of the *stars* to the ground, and *stamped* upon them”__ (Daniel 8:10).
The dragon fells a third of heaven's host not with claws but with its tail — by the prophet that teaches lies — for __“the leaders of this people cause them to err; and they that are led of them are *destroyed*”__ (Isaiah 9:16).
The trumpet armies carry the same reversal — __“their power is in their mouth, and in their *tails*: for their tails were like unto *serpents*, and had heads”__ (Revelation 9:19) — tails grown heads, which is the covenant curse in one clause: __“he shall be the head, and thou shalt be the *tail*”__ (Deuteronomy 28:44), the inversion of the blessing that made obedient Israel __“the head, and not the tail”__ (Deuteronomy 28:13).
So the command to seize the serpent by the tail is the countermove itself: take the liar's instrument in hand, and it is mastered.
The Hebrew for __“caught”__ is _chazaq_ — the very verb of the whole contest, for __“I will *harden* [chazaq] Pharaoh's heart”__ (Exodus 4:21): the hand that chazaq-grips the serpent turns it back into the staff of God; the heart that chazaq-hardens itself belongs to the serpent.
One verb, two grips.
Revelation keeps the scene for the end: __“he *laid hold on* the dragon, that old serpent… and bound him”__ (Revelation 20:2).

The rod that comes back is not bare wood.
Set overnight before the testimony, __“the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi was budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded *almonds*”__ (Numbers 17:8) — the dead stick alive, the priesthood proven by resurrection.
The almond is the _shaqed_, the watcher-tree, first to wake — __“I see a rod of an *almond tree*… for I will *watch over* my word to perform it”__ (Jeremiah 1:11-12) — and the lampstand of the sanctuary is carved as this very tree, its bowls __“made like unto *almonds*”__ (Exodus 25:33): the watcher-tree bears the sym:sym-lamp[lamp], and the lamp, Scripture says, is the commandment (Proverbs 6:23).

And mark what an almond *is*: a fruit that is itself a sym:sym-seed[seed] — and __“the seed is the *word of God*”__ (Luke 8:11).
Root to crown the watcher-tree carries nothing but the word: its blossom the priesthood's proof, its fruit the seed-word, its carved form the commandment's lampstand.
Rod, serpent, rod again — and then blossom: the priesthood cast down and gone dragon is seized at the liar's tail, restored to the Owner's palm, and buds with the resurrection sign.
The similitude that opened the first exodus is the arc of the last one.

[discrete]
=== Let My People Go — Come Out of Her

The demand carried to Pharaoh — __“let my people go, that they may serve me”__ (Exodus 8:1) — returns as the last call of the book:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 18:4]
____
And I heard another voice from heaven, saying, *Come out of her, my people*, that ye be not partakers of her sym:sym-sin[sins], and that ye receive not of her plagues.
____

Jeremiah had already given Babylon the same summons:

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 51:45]
____
*My people, go ye out of the midst of her*, and deliver ye every man his soul from the fierce anger of the LORD.
____

One voice, three ages: out of Egypt, out of Babylon, out of Babylon the great.
The people of God end every act of the story by walking out of a doomed house — and the plagues fall on those who stay.

[discrete]
=== The Spoiler from the North

Mark the quarter the destruction enters by.
__“For, lo, I will raise and cause to come up against Babylon an assembly of great nations *from the* sym:sym-north[north] *country*”__ (Jeremiah 50:9); __“a people shall come *from the north*, and a great nation”__ (Jeremiah 50:41); __“the *spoilers* shall come unto her *from the north*”__ (Jeremiah 51:48).
The word itself tells you why the destroyer owns that door.
__“North”__ — _tsaphon_ — is link:/books/symbolic-language/lucifers-declared-plan/[the hidden quarter], the lurker's quarter: the dark one, the direction the ambush comes from.footnote:fn28tsaphon[The word study — _tsaphan_, to hide by covering over, to lurk — is in the link:/books/symbolic-language/lucifers-declared-plan/[Lucifer's Declared Plan] chapter.]

The sym:sym-north[north] behaves this way throughout the prophets: __“out of the north an evil shall break forth”__ (Jeremiah 1:14) — and when the evil comes, it comes like a predator from cover, __“the sym:sym-lion[lion] is come up from his *thicket*, and the destroyer of the Gentiles is on his way”__ (Jeremiah 4:7); the *spoiler*, the robber-word, falls suddenly on the unwatchful (Jeremiah 6:22-26).
Robbers work from the dark — __“in the dark they dig through houses… they know not the light”__ (Job 24:16) — and the north is the sky's own dark, the one quarter the sun never crosses.

The word carries both of its appearances in this book at once: the *north country* is the hidden quarter where Babylon's spoilers gather, and the *sides of the north* — the uttermost recesses of that dark — are the address the enemy chose for his own seat (Lucifer’s Declared Plan).
The lurker who worked from the hidden dark is repaid out of it: the spoiler comes upon Babylon from the door she cannot watch.

[discrete]
=== The Stone That Sinks

Now the ending both stories share.
When the pursuer followed Israel into the sea, the song names his end twice: __“they *sank into the bottom as a stone*”__ (Exodus 15:5); __“they *sank as lead* in the mighty waters”__ (Exodus 15:10) — __“their persecutors thou threwest into the deeps, *as a stone* into the mighty waters”__ (Nehemiah 9:11).
Jeremiah turned that ending into a commanded sign: the scroll of Babylon’s judgment bound to a stone and thrown into Euphrates —

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 51:63-64]
____
…thou shalt bind a *stone* to it, and *cast it into the midst of Euphrates*: And thou shalt say, Thus shall *Babylon sink, and shall not rise* from the evil that I will bring upon her…
____

Revelation performs the sign at scale:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 18:21]
____
And a mighty angel took up a stone like a great *millstone*, and *cast it into the sea*, saying, Thus with violence shall that *great city* Babylon be thrown down, and shall be *found no more at all*.
____

This is a phrase-symbol in its own right — sym:sym-cast-into-sea[cast into the sea], a ruling power sunk into the sea of peoples, never to surface; the Sea study in Part Six gathers its every use.
The sym:sym-mountain[mountain] that destroyed all the earth is rolled down and burned (Jeremiah 51:25); the millstone goes under; the music stops (Revelation 18:22).

Jesus put this very sign into His disciples' mouths, twice.
__“Whosoever shall *say unto this mountain*, Be thou removed, and be thou *cast into the sea*; and shall not doubt in his heart… he shall have whatsoever he saith”__ (Mark 11:23) — and a parallel saying runs on the other kingdom-figure: __“ye might say unto this sycamine sym:sym-tree[tree], Be thou plucked up by the root, and be thou *planted in the sea*”__ (Luke 17:6).
A mountain is a kingdom and a tree is a nation; what faith commands into the sea is not landscaping — it is Babylon's sentence, spoken by the household of faith.

And Revelation shows the mechanism in order: the incense goes up __“with the *prayers of all saints*”__ (Revelation 8:3-4), the censer is cast to the earth, and at the second trumpet __“as it were a great *mountain burning with fire* was *cast into the sea*”__ (Revelation 8:8) — Jeremiah's burnt mountain, over the cliff at last.
The prayers ascend; the mountain falls.
Faith that moves mountains was never about landscaping either — it is the saints praying down the destroying mountain, and being heard.

[discrete]
=== The Verdict Is the Not-Rising

Mark the exact wording of the sentence, because the going-down is not the verdict.
Everyone in these stories goes into the waters.
Babylon sinks __“and *shall not rise*.”__

Jonah link:/books/symbolic-language/sign-of-jonah/[went into the same sea and rose]; the Messiah went into the heart of the earth and could not be held by it (Acts 2:24); and every convert enacts the split in baptism, going under into death and coming up in newness of life (Romans 6:4), his sins staying down like Babylon (Micah 7:19).footnote:fn28notrising[The rising half of the contrast is drawn scene by scene in the link:/books/symbolic-language/sign-of-jonah/[Sign of Jonah] chapter.]
The waters take everyone; the covenant decides who comes up.

The coming up is the difference between the lawless kingdom and the righteous man in the same flood — and it is why the millstone is also a personal warning: better one __“hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea”__ (Matthew 18:6) than to make the little ones stumble.
A man can be Babylon in miniature.

[discrete]
=== That Great City

Who is she?
Revelation defines both coordinates in one chapter: the sym:sym-sea[waters] where the sym:sym-harlot[whore] sitteth are the waters already identified — peoples, multitudes, and nations (Revelation 17:15) — and __“the woman which thou sawest is *that great city*, which reigneth over the kings of the earth”__ (Revelation 17:18).
The title has a history — Nineveh wore it three times (Jonah 1:2; 3:2; 4:11), and the sign-of-Jonah chapter traced where it points.
Babylon swallowed God’s people __“like a sym:sym-dragon[dragon]”__ (Jeremiah 51:34) — and the dragon, we saw with Jonah, is made to give back what it swallowed.

Revelation does more than describe the great city; it gives her street address, and gives it in the book's own symbolic grammar:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 11:8]
____
And their dead bodies shall lie in the street of the *great city*, which *spiritually is called Sodom and* sym:sym-egypt[Egypt], *where also our Lord was crucified*.
____

One city, three names.
Where was the Lord crucified? — there is one answer, and every reader knows it.
And the verse says the other two names are what that city is called *spiritually* — the very kind of name the woman wears on her forehead: __“MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF sym:sym-harlot[HARLOTS]”__ (Revelation 17:5) — a mystery-name, a spiritual name.

Nor did Revelation invent the method.
Isaiah stood in Jerusalem and addressed her rulers to their faces:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 1:10]
____
Hear the word of the LORD, ye *rulers of Sodom*; give ear unto the law of our God, ye *people of Gomorrah*.
____

Ezekiel makes the kinship formal: __“thine elder sister is Samaria… and thy younger sister… is Sodom”__ (Ezekiel 16:46).
The prophets already called Jerusalem *Sodom* when she lived like Sodom.

sym:sym-egypt[Egypt] is the same grammar.
Egypt is __“the *house of bondage*”__ (Exodus 20:2) — and Paul writes of __“Jerusalem which now is,”__ that she __“is in *bondage* with her children”__ (Galatians 4:25): the covenant city living as the slave-house is called by the slave-house's name.
Ezekiel had already watched her earn it: Jerusalem the sym:sym-harlot[harlot] __“multiplied her sym:sym-fornication[whoredoms]”__ in remembering __“the days of her youth, wherein she had played the sym:sym-harlot[harlot] *in the land of Egypt*”__ (Ezekiel 23:19).

The last identifying mark is blood.
In the great city __“was found the *blood of prophets*, and of saints”__ (Revelation 18:24) — and Jesus fixed that address for ever: __“upon you may come all the *righteous blood* shed upon the earth”__ (Matthew 23:35); __“it cannot be that a prophet perish *out of Jerusalem*”__ (Luke 13:33); __“O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that *killest the prophets*”__ (Matthew 23:37).
Sodom for her sin, Egypt for her bondage, Babylon for her boast — three spiritual names on one gate, and the street where the witnesses lie dead runs through the city that crucified her King.
The unfaithful wife of the sym:sym-marriage[marriage] chapter and the boasting queen of the widows’ chapter are the same woman, and her name is not a foreign capital's.

[discrete]
=== The Song on the Far Shore

The sea of glass scene now reads whole.
The victors stand where Israel stood — on the far side of the waters that drowned their pursuer — and they sing the same song, doubled: __“the song of Moses… and the song of the Lamb.”__
The first Exodus gave the pattern; the last performs it on every nation at once: plagues on the oppressor, a people called out, the pursuer sunk like a stone, and a shore with singing on it.
__“Thus shall Babylon sink, and shall not rise.”__
The sym:sym-gospel[gospel] the book has been reading all along ends exactly where it began at the Red sea: the kingdom that would not let go, gone under the waters — and the people of God standing on glass, dry-shod, learning the old song by heart.

sources.content:
---
title: "Mountain"
slug: mountain
order: 39
permalink: /books/symbolic-language/mountain/
description: "Scripture defines the mountain as a kingdom — Revelation, Daniel, Isaiah, and Jeremiah agree — and that one key unlocks dozens of passages, from the burning mountain cast into the sea to the command to flee to the mountains."
og_title: "Mountain — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "…the stone that smote the image became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth."
    ref: "Daniel 2:35"
---
The first case study is __“mountain,”__ which represents kingdoms or power structures.
The pyramid-like structure of a mountain mirrors the power structure of delegated authority and is an apt analogy — but subjective aptness is not a basis for defining a symbol.
Thankfully, in this case Scripture comes right out and defines it:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 17:9-10]
____
This calls for a mind with wisdom.
The seven heads are *seven mountains* on which the woman sits.
They are also *seven kings* (kingdoms).
____

Revelation tells us that mountains mean kingdoms, and by analogy hills are cities.
The question is whether Scripture consistently uses mountain with the same symbolic meaning, or whether this is a one-off.
Other times in Scripture we are given a vision and an interpretation, which establishes the definition by analogy:

[quote.scripture, Daniel 2:35 (NKJV)]
____
Then the iron, the clay, the bronze, the silver, and the gold were crushed together, and became like sym:sym-chaff[chaff] from the summer threshing floors; the sym:sym-wind[wind] carried them away so that no trace of them was found.
And the sym:sym-stone[stone] that struck the sym:sym-image[image] became a *great mountain* and *filled the whole earth*.
____

[quote.scripture, Daniel 2:44-45 (NKJV)]
____
And in the days of these kings the God of heaven will set up a *kingdom* which shall never be destroyed; and the kingdom shall not be left to other people; it shall break in pieces and *consume all these kingdoms*, and it shall stand forever.
Inasmuch as you saw that the sym:sym-stone[stone] was cut out of the *mountain* without hands, and that it broke in pieces the iron, the bronze, the clay, the silver, and the gold — the great God has made known to the king what will come to pass after this.
The dream is certain, and its interpretation is sure.
____

In this case Daniel explains a vision of a statue with layers of gold, silver, bronze, and feet of clay and iron, and explains that this statue represents successive kingdoms.
Then a final kingdom comes and destroys the statue and rules for ever and ever.
The final kingdom of the statue is consumed when God’s kingdom comes as a stone that grows into a mountain over the entire earth.

The sym:sym-stone[stone] itself repays a closer look.
It is __“cut out… without hands”__ (Daniel 2:45) — and _to cut_ link:/books/symbolic-language/daniel-unsealed/[is the covenant verb] (Genesis 15:18).footnote:fn33karath[Covenants are cut, not made — _karath_ — as the link:/books/symbolic-language/daniel-unsealed/[Daniel Unsealed] chapter showed.]
A stone cut by no human hand is a covenant cut by God Himself — and Scripture names the sym:sym-rock[Rock]: __“that sym:sym-rock[Rock] was Christ”__ (1 Corinthians 10:4), the covenant in person; __“the sym:sym-stone[stone] which the builders refused”__ is become __“the head stone of the corner”__ (Psalm 118:22).
So the stone and the rock are the covenant, and the mountain it grows into is that covenant become a kingdom over all the earth.

[quote.scripture, Daniel 2:38-39 (NKJV)]
____
You are this head of gold.
After you shall arise another *kingdom* inferior to yours; then another, a third *kingdom* of bronze, which shall *rule over all the earth*.
____

The fact that the mountain is described as growing and covering the entire earth is another clue that this isn’t a physical mountain.
The analogy from Daniel is carried on in Isaiah.

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 2:2-3]
____
It shall come to pass in the latter days that the *mountain* of the house of the Lord shall be established as the highest of the *mountains*, and shall be lifted up above the *hills*; and all the *nations* shall flow to it, and many peoples shall come.
____

See the same symbolic meaning applied in Jeremiah, describing Babylon the Great, which rules over the whole earth and destroys nation after nation.
Here Jeremiah tells us this destroying mountain will become a burnt mountain.

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 51:25]
____
“Behold, I am against you, O *destroying mountain*, Who destroys all the earth,” says the Lord.
“And I will stretch out My hand against you, Roll you down from the rocks, And make you a *burnt mountain*.”
____

Now we have Daniel, Revelation, Isaiah, and Jeremiah all agreeing on the meaning of this symbol of a Mountain as a Kingdom.
With this knowledge we can now gain greater insight into many other scriptures.
Consider the account in Revelation of a flaming mountain thrown into the sea:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 8:8-9]
____
Then the second angel sounded his trumpet, and something like a *huge mountain*, all ablaze, was *thrown into the* sym:sym-sea[sea].
A third of the *sea* turned into blood, a third of the *living creatures* in the sea died….
____

To gauge how this verse is usually read, I asked Claude, as before, to name the most common explanations of this __“mountain”__ and estimate how prevalent each one is.
By this estimate, about 85% miss the symbolic meaning here:

.How the “mountain” is usually read (Rev. 8:8)
[.prevalence-table%unbreakable, frame=topbot, grid=none, cols="^2,6,^2", options="header"]
|===
| Rank | Common interpretation | Est. %

| 1 | Literal asteroid or meteor impact | 40%
| 2 | Literal volcano hurled into the sea | 25%
| 3 | Nuclear blast or modern warfare | 20%
| 4 | A nation or world empire | 15%
|===

How do we know that this isn’t a literal mountain in this context?
The answer is in the phrase __“thrown into the sea,”__ the __“sea turning into blood,”__ and the __“creatures in the sea,”__ all in the same sentence.
In a later chapter I will show the evidence that sym:sym-sea[sea] is a symbol that means the masses of people, the population of the earth, and that sym:sym-living[living creatures], sym:sym-beast[beast], and sym:sym-beast[animals] represent gentile nations.

Symbolically, Revelation 8:8-9 is saying that when a __“huge mountain”__ — a world empire — is thrown down, a third of the people will die and a third of the nations will be destroyed.
This implies that on the order of two billion people will die when this mountain is thrown down.

One final supporting piece of evidence is that a __“stone, rock, mountain, etc.”__ being __“thrown into the sea”__ to __“never rise again”__ is the prophetic symbol tied to the fall of Babylon the Great.
And thus symbols can be composed of both words and catch-phrases.

[quote.scripture, Matthew 17:20]
____
So Jesus said to them, “Because of your unbelief; for assuredly, I say to you, if you have sym:sym-faith[faith] *as a mustard* sym:sym-seed[seed], you will say to this *mountain*, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move; and nothing will be impossible for you.”
____

[quote.scripture, Matthew 21:21]
____
So Jesus answered and said to them, “Assuredly, I say to you, if you have sym:sym-faith[faith] and do not doubt, you will not only do what was done to the sym:sym-fig[*fig tree*], but also if you say to this *mountain*, ‘Be removed and be *cast into the* sym:sym-sea[sea],’ it will be done.”
____

[quote.scripture, Mark 11:23]
____
For assuredly, I say to you, whoever says to this *mountain*, ‘Be removed and be *cast into the sea*,’ and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that those things he says will be done, he will have whatever he says.
____

Once again I asked Claude to rank how this __“mountain”__ is understood, and a national power sits at the very bottom of the list — so low it barely registers:

.How the “mountain” Jesus moves is usually read
[.prevalence-table%unbreakable, frame=topbot, grid=none, cols="^2,6,^2", options="header"]
|===
| Rank | Common interpretation | Est. %

| 1 | A personal obstacle or problem | 55%
| 2 | A literal mountain (hyperbole) | 25%
| 3 | The Mount of Olives / Temple Mount | 8%
| 4 | A spiritual stronghold or doubt | 6%
| 5 | The corrupt temple/religious system | 4%
| 6 | A national power or kingdom | 2%
|===

How do we know that this mountain is not a literal mountain, or merely an impossible obstacle, in this context?
Because the context is a fig tree and a mustard tree — and sym:sym-tree[trees] are another symbol that Scripture defines as kingdoms or nations — and of course __“thrown into the sea”__ is a symbol clearly referring to Babylon the Great, as the link:/books/symbolic-language/the-fall-of-babylon/[Fall of Babylon] chapter demonstrated — and as the next chapter will trace from the Song of the Sea onward.

What we learn from this is that the symbolic language of the Bible is interconnected: symbols are defined in terms of symbols and phrases, as well as the verbs, adjectives, and other personifications used with the symbol.
For this reason, we often see the same set of symbols connected over and over.

[quote.scripture, Psalm 46:2-3]
____
Though the *mountains* be carried into the midst of the sym:sym-sea[sea]; though the waters thereof roar and be troubled, though the *mountains* shake with the swelling thereof.
____

.How the “mountains” are usually read (Ps. 46)
[.prevalence-table%unbreakable, frame=topbot, grid=none, cols="^2,6,^2", options="header"]
|===
| Rank | Common interpretation | Est. %

| 1 | Literal earthquakes or natural disaster | 40%
| 2 | Life’s troubles and instability | 27%
| 3 | Cosmic or end-times upheaval | 18%
| 4 | Nations or kingdoms shaken | 15%
|===

Once again, by Claude’s estimate, the symbolic meaning is missed by roughly 85% of those who interpret the verse.
Now consider this poetic picture from Joel:

[quote.scripture, Joel 2:2]
____
A day of darkness and gloom, A day of sym:sym-cloud[clouds] and of thick [dark] mist, Like the *dawn* spread over the *mountains*;
____

The picture is of __“dawn,”__ __“mist,”__ or __“fog”__ spread over the __“mountains,”__ which is quite common in early morning and aligns with the visual of a __“day of clouds and thick dark mist.”__
The Hebrew word for __“dawn,”__ _shachar_, link:/books/symbolic-language/lucifers-declared-plan/[names the dark before sunrise].footnote:fn33shachar[Derived — _shachar_ written on the letters of blackness — in the link:/books/symbolic-language/lucifers-declared-plan/[Lucifer's Declared Plan] chapter.] It names the first light while the sky is still quite dark, before the sun burns away the fog.
Now, with the greater context, we have dark clouds of smoke spread over the nations.
This is just one of dozens of verses that gain new meaning when you apply the symbolic meaning of mountain.

[quote.scripture, Matthew 24:15-16]
____
So when you see the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea *flee to the mountains*.
____

Here is a verse that contains instructions for the future, and to understand the instructions it is helpful to know that __“mountains”__ means nations.
In other words: get out of Judea.
In AD 70, those who survived the fall of Jerusalem were scattered to the nations, so this prophecy has been fulfilled in this sense already.

[quote.scripture, Luke 21:20-21]
____
When you see Jerusalem being surrounded by armies, you will know that its desolation is near.
Then let those who are in Judea *flee to the mountains*, let those in the *city* get out, and let those in the country not enter the city.
____

Another verse sounds poetic on the surface, but carries a far more practical message when read by Scripture’s own symbols:

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 50:6]
____
My people have been sym:sym-lost[lost sheep]; their *shepherds* have led them astray, in the *mountains* they have turned them away. *From mountain to hill* they have gone; they have forgotten their resting place.
____

Here His people are the sheep; the shepherds are the pastors and teachers who led people astray among the nations they were scattered to.
His people have gone from nation to city and have forgotten their home.

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 40:4]
____
Every sym:sym-valley[valley] shall be exalted, and every *mountain and hill* shall be made low.
____

This verse from Isaiah now has far deeper meaning: the nations and cities will be humbled (brought low).
And those who are humble, obedient even to death, will be exalted and lifted up.
The mountains are high places, proud places, and they contrast with their opposite, the valleys — those enslaved by the mountains.

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 16:16]
____
Behold, I will send for many *fishers*, said the LORD, and they shall fish them; and after will I send for many *hunters*, and they shall hunt them from *every mountain*, and from *every hill*, and out of the *holes of the rocks*.
____

Here is another case where mountains (nations) are used with other symbols: fishermen and hunters.
Here Jeremiah is prophesying about Jesus calling people to be fishers of men.
Then, those who are not caught as fish will be hunted down from among the nations, in every city, and out of every bunker.
The holes of the rocks are then referenced in Revelation:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 6:14-16]
____
And the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together; and *every mountain and* sym:sym-island[island] were moved out of their places.
And the kings of the earth, and the great men, and the rich men, and the chief captains, and the mighty men, and every slave, and every free man, hid themselves in the dens and in the *rocks of the mountains*; and said to the *mountains and rocks*, Fall on us, and hide us.
____

Now that you know that mountain means a kingdom, we should ask ourselves: what does an sym:sym-island[island] represent?

[quote.scripture, Revelation 16:19-20]
____
And great *Babylon* came in remembrance before God, to give to her the cup of the wine of the fierceness of his wrath.
And *every* sym:sym-island[island] *fled away*, and the *mountains were not found*.
____

Are literal mountains going to disappear, or is this clearly talking about the third of the nations thrown into the sea, never to rise again?
When I read this, it struck me as odd that an island could flee, or escape.
It is the personification of island that led me to research the sym:sym-island[island] symbol, which we will cover in a future chapter.

I will close this chapter on mountains with one final notable use, when Jesus was tested in the desert:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 4:8]
____
Again, the devil takes him up into an *exceeding high mountain*, and shows him *all the kingdoms of the world*, and the glory of them;
____

Here we see an exceedingly high mountain from which all the other kingdoms of the earth can be seen.
In other words, he is taken to a kingdom ruling over all the other kings of the earth — likely Babylon the Great.

By now you should see the pattern: Scripture reliably and consistently uses the word mountain as a way to say __“nation”__ or __“kingdom”__ in many different contexts across the whole of Scripture.
I have only addressed a few of the notable uses, but once you internalize this symbol you will find it used in countless other places in profound ways.

In the process of exploring the mountain symbol, we came across many other symbols: the sym:sym-sea[sea] (the masses of mankind), the hills (cities), the sym:sym-tree[tree] and the fig tree (kingdoms and Israel), the stone and the rock (the covenant), the sym:sym-beast[beasts] and living creatures (the gentile nations), the sym:sym-island[island], the fishers and the hunters, the valley, and Babylon the Great.
The sea, the trees and their beasts, and the island are taken up in the chapters just ahead, each defined the same way we defined the mountain — by letting Scripture interpret Scripture.
Babylon the Great we have already traced through Part Five, and the glossary carries the rest.

A word, then, about what we have just done with AI.
Left to its own intuition, the AI missed the plain meaning of the mountain in nearly every verse — it simply returned the common teachings the tables above record.
Yet the moment it was given the process to follow, and made to follow it step by step, the same meaning became clear and all but deterministic.

The contrast matters: AI does not interpret Scripture for us, and it must not be trusted to — but the meaning is already there, recoverable by anyone, or anything, willing to follow the method rather than lean on inherited opinion.
What forces the right answer is not the cleverness of the reader but the discipline of the process.

sources.content:
---
title: "Sea & Waters"
slug: sea-and-waters
order: 40
permalink: /books/symbolic-language/sea-and-waters/
description: "If mountains are kingdoms, the sea is the peoples they rise from and rule over. Revelation 17 defines both — the waters are 'peoples, and multitudes, and nations, and tongues' — and that key unlocks the beasts from the sea, the flood that is an invading army, the two waters of creation — a restless sea of nations below, and the sea of glass above where the redeemed stand — and the 'no more sea' of the new creation."
og_title: "Sea & Waters — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "The LORD on high is mightier than the noise of many waters, yea, than the mighty waves of the sea."
    ref: "Psalm 93:4"
---
The next symbol we will investigate is the sea.
The sea is a symbol that comes up over and over again in Scripture.
From the beasts coming out of the sea, to mountains and trees being thrown into the sea, to Jonah, and then Jesus walking on the sea, and disciples fishing in the sea.
Understanding how its symbolic meaning is consistent across so many different situations is critical for understanding the prophecies, miracles, and less notable references to the sea.

The sea is sometimes called sym:sym-sea[waters] or sym:sym-sea[waves] and is related to sym:sym-flood[floods].
This chapter gathers those uses and shows how they clarify verses often read as mere poetic ornament.

Like the _mountain_ symbol, Scripture directly tells us the meaning of “waters” and “sea” in several different verses across the Old and New Testaments.
Let’s start with Revelation.

[quote.scripture, Revelation 17:1]
____
…the judgment of the great sym:sym-harlot[whore] that sitteth upon sym:sym-sea[many waters]:
____

[quote.scripture, Revelation 17:15]
____
And he saith unto me, The sym:sym-sea[waters] which thou sawest, where the sym:sym-harlot[whore] sitteth, are *peoples, and multitudes, and nations, and tongues*.
____

Here we do not have to guess: the messenger is interpreting the vision for John, just as he interpreted the seven mountains a few verses earlier.
The waters are peoples, multitudes, nations, and tongues — humanity in the mass, described four ways so that nothing slips between the words.

Notice that this is the very same chapter that defined the mountain (Revelation 17:9-10).
One chapter of Revelation hands us both halves of the map: the woman sits on seven sym:sym-mountain[mountains] — kingdoms — and upon sym:sym-sea[many waters] — the peoples those kingdoms rise from and rule over.
In the mountain chapter I deferred the evidence that the sea means the masses of people; this chapter is that evidence.

The picture is natural enough that English keeps it to this day: we still speak of a sea of faces, a wave of immigration, a flood of refugees.
But as we learned with the mountain, an apt analogy is not the basis for defining a symbol — and neither is a familiar idiom.
The question is whether Scripture itself uses the sea this way consistently, or whether Revelation 17 is a one-off.

In answering it I can show you one of the most useful tools for discovering symbols on your own: Hebrew poetry rhymes ideas instead of sounds.
A verse says a thing once, then says it again in other words — so the second line is an inspired gloss on the first, Scripture defining its own terms in parallel columns.
Watch Isaiah do it:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 17:12-13]
____
Woe to the multitude of *many people*, which make a noise like the noise of the sym:sym-sea[seas]; and to the rushing of *nations*, that make a rushing like the rushing of mighty sym:sym-sea[waters]!
The *nations* shall rush like the rushing of sym:sym-sea[many waters]…
____

People are set against seas; nations against waters.
The Psalms do the same:

[quote.scripture, Psalm 65:7]
____
Which stilleth the noise of the sym:sym-sea[seas], the noise of their sym:sym-sea[waves], and the *tumult of the people*.
____

Seas, waves, and the tumult of the people — three phrases, one meaning.
Once you know to look for these parallel columns, definitions turn up in verses you have sung right past.
Here is one sitting in plain sight in a praise psalm:

[quote.scripture, Psalm 98:7]
____
Let the sym:sym-sea[sea] roar, and the *fulness thereof*; the *world*, and *they that dwell therein*.
____

The sea is matched to the world, and the fulness of the sea to they that dwell in the world.
What fills the sea is people.

The witnesses are not a handful of hand-picked verses.
The word __“sea”__ appears in 376 verses of Scripture, and __“waters”__ and __“floods”__ in hundreds more.
Gather the sea verses and sort them, and the shape of the whole is striking: roughly three of every four either connect the sea to people outright, put the symbol to work — kingdoms rising out of it, armies as floods, men as fish, multitudes as sand — or take on a second depth once the symbol is known.
Only about eighty are plain geography: borders, coastlines, harbors, and shipping.
No figure of speech stays that consistent by accident — dozens of authors, some fifteen centuries apart, all speaking one vocabulary.

[quote.scripture, Daniel 7:2-3]

And four great sym:sym-beast[beasts] came up from the sym:sym-sea[sea], diverse one from another.

Empires do not fall from the sky; they take shape out of the churning mass of peoples.

What churns the mass?
The four winds of heaven — the __“four spirits of the heavens, which go forth from standing before the Lord of all the earth”__ (Zechariah 6:5) — for throughout Scripture sym:sym-wind[wind] is spirit.
Unseen powers sent from God’s throne agitate the nations, and out of the agitation kingdoms rise.
The winds had their chapter at the head of Part Five; here it is enough to see the pattern working.

And I stood upon the sym:sym-sand[sand] of the sym:sym-sea[sea], and saw a sym:sym-beast[beast] rise up out of the sym:sym-sea[sea], having seven heads and ten horns…

____
So is this great and wide sym:sym-sea[sea], wherein are sym:sym-beast[things creeping] innumerable, both *small and great* sym:sym-beast[beasts].

Small beasts and great — petty powers and empires — swarming in the sea of peoples, with the sym:sym-dragon[dragon] himself at play among them.

[quote.scripture, Revelation 16:3]

And the second angel poured out his vial upon the sym:sym-sea[sea]; and it became as the *blood of a dead man*: and *every living soul died* in the sym:sym-sea[sea].
____

Souls live in this sea.
No literal ocean has souls in it; the sea of peoples has nothing else.

There is a particular motion of this sea to watch for.
When the waters rise, overflow, and sweep across the land, the symbol is a nation on the move — an invading army.
Isaiah names the flood outright:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 8:7]
____
…the Lord bringeth up upon them the sym:sym-flood[waters of the river], strong and many, *even the king of Assyria*, and all his glory…
____

The flood is the king of Assyria — the verse says so in the same breath — and the next verse follows the water up to Judah’s neck: __“he shall overflow and go over, he shall reach even to the neck”__ (Isaiah 8:8).
Egypt gets the same picture, and this time the flood speaks:

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 46:7-8]
____
Who is this that cometh up as a sym:sym-flood[flood], whose sym:sym-sea[waters] are moved as the rivers?
*Egypt* riseth up like a sym:sym-flood[flood], and his waters are moved like the rivers; and he saith, I will go up, and will *cover the earth*; I will *destroy the city and the inhabitants* thereof.
____

A flood that talks, boasts, and plans a campaign is not weather.
Jeremiah asks the riddle — who is this flood? — and answers it in the next line: Egypt.
